He wore a white vest washed yellow, a grey long-sleeved work jacket over it with the cuffs rolled to the forearm, the flesh of his forearms in lumps, tanned the colour of soy sauce, veins coiled over them like old tree roots. His trouser legs were covered in grey-white cement stains, and his canvas army shoes had split at the sides and been sewn up with black thread.

He was around fifty, hair cropped so short you could see his scalp, his temples already white. His face was square, with high cheekbones; the corners of his eyes drooped, and the corners of his mouth drooped too, so that he always looked a little aggrieved.

He had his cigarettes out before he even reached the discipline office door, a pack of Hongtashan, opened, seven or eight left inside. He pulled one out and offered it to Mr. Sun with both hands, bending at the waist, bending deep.

“Mr. Sun, Mr. Sun, sorry for the trouble, sorry for the trouble.”

Mr. Sun didn’t take the cigarette and waved it away. Gu Jianguo wasn’t embarrassed in the least. He tucked the cigarette behind his ear and rubbed his hands on his trousers, rubbing off a layer of dust.

“The child doesn’t know any better, she’s caused you trouble.” His voice was low, with a heavy accent, the end of every sentence sinking. “Our family’s not well off, her mother passed early, there’s nobody to look after her, I’m out working all day and haven’t been able to… It’s my fault for not raising her right, my fault.”

When he said “her mother passed early,” Gu Xuerong, standing in the corner of the office, moved her eyes.

Her mother hadn’t passed. Her mother was in the city, living with another man in a flat with a lift. They had a son, who was in Year Two of primary school this year.

She said nothing.

“This cleaning duty, she has to do it.” Mr. Sun sat behind his desk and tapped the desktop with a finger. “This is no small matter. If a person won’t even take on their share for the collective, what will become of them in society? Our school has its limits too. If someone won’t mend their ways, then we advise them to leave.”

“Yes, yes, yes,” said Gu Jianguo, nodding again and again. “She should be punished, she should. However you say to punish her, Mr. Sun.”

“Take her home for today and let her reflect for a day. From tomorrow, as I said, a week of cleaning duty. A three-thousand-character self-criticism, due Monday.”

“Yes, yes, yes.”

Gu Jianguo bowed again. As he bent, he glanced back at Gu Xuerong.

The glance was very short, quickly withdrawn. When he turned back, it was the same drooping, slightly aggrieved, honest man’s face again.

But Gu Xuerong had seen it.

She knew that glance far too well.

## 3. Back Street

From the school to the dormitory, Back Street was the shortest way.

Not yet eleven in the morning, and Back Street wasn’t properly awake. The braised-meat stall wasn’t set up; there was only a damp patch of ground with a few plastic crates turned upside down on it. The mahjong parlour’s door curtain was rolled halfway up, dark inside, and someone was sweeping, the broom scraping the concrete, swish, swish. The copy shop’s glass door was open, the copiers humming. The curtains on the second floor were drawn, forest green, perfectly still.

Gu Jianguo walked ahead with long strides, his soles slapping the ground, slap, slap.

Out of the school gate, across the road, into Back Street, past the copy shop, to the first corner, until the school wall could no longer be seen behind them.

He stopped and turned round.

“You fucking—”

He didn’t shout it. He forced it out through his teeth, kept very low, low as a stone sinking to the bottom of the water.

“I carry three hundred bags of cement a day, carry them till I can’t straighten my back, to earn those few coins to pay for your schooling. And you go and shame me like this at school? Won’t even sweep a floor? Who do you think you are, a princess?”

Gu Xuerong stood in front of him, two steps away.

Her schoolbag was on one shoulder, the strap slipped down to her elbow. She didn’t pull it back up.

“Talk! Gone dumb?”

“You’re just like your mother.” Gu Jianguo’s voice was creeping up, bit by bit. “Ungrateful, the pair of you. Can’t be tamed. Your mother was exactly the same, lazy, useless at everything, and in the end she just walked off and left me with a money-losing girl like you—”

The owner of a breakfast stall across the street poked her head out, looked, and pulled it back in.

“How much have I spent on you? Have you added it up? School fees, living money, you running off to the hospital every few days, drips, medicine, which of those doesn’t cost money?” He took a step forward, a step that brought him very close, so close that his smell of cement and sweat suddenly covered everything. “I’m telling you, if you can’t make it at school, then stop going. If you can’t make it, get married early. Married at eighteen. I’ve already asked around about the bride price. Back home a girl gets at least a hundred and eighty-eight thousand these days. With a body like yours, knock a bit off, a hundred and twenty, thirty thousand at least—”

Gu Xuerong looked at him.

There was no expression on her face. Not the kind of nothing that comes from holding something in, but real nothing, like a wall that everything slides off and nothing sticks to. She watched his mouth open and shut, watched the white froth at the corners of it, watched a vein swell on his forehead, watched the Hongtashan tucked behind his ear, which trembled as he talked and was about to fall.

She was wondering when the cigarette would fall.

She could barely even hear what he was saying any more. She had heard those words many times: on the phone, at the dinner table when she went back for New Year, on the night she was twelve and had a fever of thirty-nine degrees and he got so fed up with her crying that he locked her outside. “Money-losing girl,” “just like your mother,” “can’t be tamed,” “get married”—she had known them by heart for a long time, known them by heart until they weren’t words any more, just sounds, mixed in with the swish of the broom on Back Street, the hum of the copiers, the horn of a tricycle in the distance, a buzzing like rain.

“What are you staring at? You’ve got the nerve to look at me?”

Her right hand was in her sleeve, gripping her left wrist through the fabric, very tightly.

## 4. Chen Xi

“Uncle.”

A voice cut in from the side.

“Pretty loud, yelling at your own daughter in the middle of the street.”

Gu Jianguo’s head whipped round.

Outside the internet café with no sign on Back Street stood someone. Skinny, long neck, school jacket unzipped and hanging open over a black T-shirt with a skull on it. In his hand was a bottle of iced tea, beaded with condensation that was dripping off it.

It was Chen Xi.

He had slipped out in first period. Maths, which he didn’t understand and didn’t want to listen to. He had told his deskmate he was going to the toilet, gone downstairs the moment he was out of the classroom, and climbed the stretch of wall behind the canteen that had no glass on it. He had played games in the internet café for two hours and come out to buy a drink, and as he pushed the door open he heard the yelling outside.

He recognised Gu Xuerong.

He also recognised the words that had just come out of this man’s mouth.

“Who are you?” Gu Jianguo looked him up and down. “What’s it got to do with you?”

“Nothing to do with me.” Chen Xi unscrewed the iced tea and took a swig. “Just annoying to listen to. Uncle, she’s your daughter, not your livestock. At school you’re all bows and scrapes to the teachers, and the moment you’re out the gate you take it out on her. You really know how to pick the soft target, don’t you.”

Gu Jianguo’s face flushed red in an instant.

He looked at Chen Xi, then at Gu Xuerong, then at Chen Xi again, his eyes slowly narrowing. Something surfaced in those drooping eyes, murky and thick.

“Oh—” he drew the word out. “So that’s it. So that’s why she doesn’t do anything proper at school. She’s been carrying on with someone outside.”

He turned to Gu Xuerong and jabbed a finger at Chen Xi:

“This is the one you’re keeping on the side, is it? Eh? So young and already up to no good, exactly like your mother, the minute she sees a man—”

Chen Xi threw his iced tea on the ground.

The bottle bounced once on the concrete and rolled away, red tea spilling all over the ground.

His punch was very fast and very straight, and it landed on Gu Jianguo’s cheekbone.

Gu Jianguo’s head jerked to one side.

Only once.

Then it came back. There wasn’t even much sign of pain on his face, just a red patch on the cheekbone. He looked at Chen Xi the way you’d look at a cat that had pounced on you.

Chen Xi froze for half a second.

Half a second was all it took. Gu Jianguo reached out and grabbed him by the collar, gripping hard, his fist jammed under Chen Xi’s chin, and lifted. Chen Xi was one metre seventy-eight, and he was hoisted until his heels left the ground. He tried to pry the hand off; it was like a vice and didn’t budge.

“You little shit,” said Gu Jianguo. “You dare raise a hand to me?”

His other hand balled into a fist and slammed into Chen Xi’s stomach.

Chen Xi folded up like a shrimp.

There was nothing fancy about that punch; it was just heavy. The heaviness of twenty years of carrying cement, coming up from the waist, through the shoulder, through that vein-coiled arm, all the way into the fist. Chen Xi’s mouth hung open with no sound coming out, and only after two seconds did he drag in a breath, a breath that sounded like cloth tearing.

Gu Jianguo let go of his collar. Chen Xi dropped to his knees, one hand braced on the ground, one hand clutching his stomach, his face grey-green, his forehead against the concrete, in the puddle of iced tea he had just thrown.

Gu Jianguo raised his foot.

“—Abiao!”

Chen Xi yelled it from the ground. His voice was hoarse, with a hint of tears in it, but it was loud, loud enough for the whole of Back Street to hear.

“Abiao! Beanpole! Get the fuck out here!”

The thick plastic curtain of the internet café was flung aside.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Four of them came out.

In front was one with yellow hair, dyed like a bundle of autumn straw, an inch of black already grown out at the roots, wearing a basketball vest washed out of shape, with a half-peeled temporary tattoo on his arm: a dragon, only the tail left. He was called Abiao, seventeen, had quit school in the second year of middle school, and now kept order in the internet café for the owner and slept at night on the long sofa at the very back.

Behind him came a tall skinny one, tall as a washing pole, whom everyone called Beanpole. A chubby one with a round face and a silver stud in one ear that glinted in the sun. And a smallest one who looked fourteen or fifteen at most, only up to Abiao’s shoulder, still holding a game controller he hadn’t had time to put down.

None of them were from No. 8 High. Most had stopped school halfway through middle school and drifted around this back street, drifted for two or three years, until they had become part of the street, like the internet café, the braised-meat stall and the crooked telegraph poles.

Abiao glanced at Chen Xi on his knees, then at Gu Jianguo.

He didn’t ask a single thing.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

The fight was nothing like as good-looking as on TV.

Nobody struck a pose, nobody shouted a slogan. Abiao threw himself at Gu Jianguo from the side and grabbed him round the waist; Beanpole locked one of his arms from behind; Chubby pinned the other; the smallest one hesitated, stuffed the controller in his pocket, and threw himself at one of Gu Jianguo’s legs.

Gu Jianguo was very strong. He shook himself once and Beanpole was thrown back two staggering steps, then lunged in again. He shook again, Chubby’s ear stud got yanked and he yelped with pain, and didn’t let go.

The four of them, bit by bit, pressed him down. Like a few ants dragging a beetle much bigger than themselves.

In the end he went down. On his side, his face against the concrete of Back Street, against the patch where the iced tea had spilled, the red tea soaking half his face.

He struggled underneath them, panting, swearing in ugly words, each one filthier than the last. The four of them held him down. None of them hit him. They just held him down, held him tight.

Chen Xi got up off the ground.

He was still clutching his stomach, his face still grey-green, a trail of spit at the corner of his mouth, or blood; he wiped it off with his sleeve. He walked over and crouched in front of Gu Jianguo, very low, low enough to look that face pressed against the ground in the eye.

“Old man,” he said, breathing hard. “Still putting on a show for me, are you.”

He grinned, a very ugly grin, a bit of red on his teeth.

“I’m the best fighter round here.”

On top of Gu Jianguo’s back, Abiao snorted out a laugh.

“You, the best fighter?” he said. “The way you were on your knees just now, you looked like my gran’s dog.”

“Shut up,” said Chen Xi. “Let me keep a bit of face.”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Gu Xuerong hadn’t moved from where she stood.

From the moment her father started cursing her, to Chen Xi’s iced tea smashing on the ground, to her father being pinned down, she had stood at that corner, at that distance of two steps, and not moved once.

Her schoolbag still hung from her elbow, the strap cutting into her sleeve.

She looked at her father’s face pressed against the ground. She had been looking at that face for sixteen years: had seen it flushed red with drink at the dinner table, seen it creased all over with smiles for relatives at New Year, seen its eyebrows lift on the phone as it said the words “bride price.” She had never seen it from this angle. From above, looking down at it pressed into a pool of red iced tea, watching its mouth curse, spit and tea mixing together, watching its drooping eye roll up and find her.

The Hongtashan finally fell from behind his ear, landed on the ground, rolled half a turn, and soaked in the tea, the paper slowly turning brown.

She had been waiting for it to fall the whole time.

Now it had.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

“That’s enough.” Chen Xi stood up and brushed the dust off his knees. “Let him go.”

The four of them looked at each other, let go one by one, and stepped back two paces.

Gu Jianguo got up off the ground. He got up very slowly: first one arm braced, then his knees, and only then did he stand. His work jacket was covered in dust, half his face was wet, there was a swelling on his cheekbone, but apart from that he didn’t seem to be hurt anywhere. He stood there panting, looking at these young men half a head shorter than him.

He looked at Chen Xi, then at the other four, clenched his fists, and unclenched them. Across the road, the woman from the breakfast stall had poked her head out again, still holding a spatula.

His eyes turned back to Gu Xuerong.

“You just wait.”

His voice was very low, low enough that only she could make it out.

“I don’t believe you’ll never come home.”

He bent down, picked up the soaked cigarette, looked at it, and threw it away. He turned and walked off towards the end of Back Street, still with long strides, his soles slapping the ground, slap, slap, only dragging a little more than when he came, a slight limp in his left foot.

At the end of the street he stopped for a moment without looking back. Then he turned the corner and was gone.

Abiao spat after him, “Ptui,” then looked at Chen Xi. “Who was that?”

“No idea,” said Chen Xi.

“No idea, and you went for him?”

“Didn’t like the look of him.”

Abiao looked at him for a while, then at the girl standing at the corner, said “Ah,” and asked nothing more.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Gu Xuerong was still standing in the same place.

Chen Xi walked over and stopped a metre in front of her. The corner of his mouth was split, a thin cut oozing threads of blood; he hadn’t noticed.

“You all right?”

She looked at him.

The way she looked at him gave Chen Xi the creeps a little. It wasn’t fear, it wasn’t gratitude, nor what you’d expect from someone who had had a fright. Her eyes were very level, very still, like a pool where nothing you threw in would make a ripple.

After a few seconds, she spoke.

“You’re bleeding.”

Chen Xi paused, reached up to the corner of his mouth and found a bit of red. “…Oh. It’s nothing.”

She looked down and took a packet of tissues from the side pocket of her schoolbag. The very cheapest kind, fifty fen a packet, a faded peony printed on the wrapper. She pulled one out and held it out to him.

The hand holding out the tissue was trembling.

A very fine tremble, like a leaf in the wind, that you wouldn’t notice unless you looked closely. Chen Xi noticed. When he took the tissue his fingertips touched hers, cold as if just out of the fridge.

He said nothing and pressed the tissue to the corner of his mouth.

“…Thanks.”

## 5. Group Chat

Ye Zhixing was in chemistry.

The chemistry teacher was balancing equations on the board, tapping with the chalk, explaining the gain and loss of electrons in redox reactions. The classroom was stuffy. The windows were open, but there was no breeze, and the plane leaves outside hung perfectly still.

Gu Xuerong’s seat was empty. Her maths book from the morning still lay open on her desk, the scrap of paper with the parabola on top of it, one corner fluttering in the draught from the ceiling fan.

The phone in his desk buzzed.

It was the class group chat. The group was called “Year One Class Seven (No Teachers),” forty-odd people, mostly used for posting homework answers and stickers.

Chen Xi had posted:

> @Ye Zhixing something happened check your DMs  

It was followed by a friend request. The verification message was just two words: Chen Xi.

Ye Zhixing looked at the group message for two seconds. People quickly replied in the group: “What happened?” “???” “Chen Xi, what have you done now?” Chen Xi ignored them, and the message was soon pushed up out of sight by the stickers that followed.

He accepted the friend request.

A voice message came through at once. He put an earbud in his right ear, propped the phone upright behind his textbook, held the message down and listened to it all.

Fifty-nine seconds.

Then another. Forty-two seconds.

Then a photo: the corner of Back Street, a pool of red liquid on the ground, a sodden cigarette soaking in it.

Then a line of text:

> we took her to get food dont worry shes ok  

Ye Zhixing put the phone face down on his desk.

At the front, the chemistry teacher turned round, looked at the class and said, “This problem. Anyone want to come up and do it?”

Nobody raised a hand.

Ye Zhixing stood up.

The chemistry teacher’s eyes lit up. “Ye Zhixing? Good, come on up—”

“I need the toilet.”

He went out of the back door.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

The toilets were at the end of the corridor. He didn’t go in. He stood at the window outside them, where a layer of dust had settled on the sill; someone had written “FUCK” in the dust with a finger, and someone else had crossed it out with another.

He rang Uncle He.

“Young master.”

“Uncle He.” His voice was very level, so level it didn’t sound quite like him. “Last month, the homeroom teacher of No. 8 High, Year One Class Seven, had six students come to his place one weekend to move furniture. Sixth floor, no lift.”

There was silence on the line for a while.

“Do you know which estate?”

“No,” he said. “There’s a student called Chen Xi, you can ask him. He should have photos on his phone. They took a group photo after the move, Mr. Sun told them to, said he’d post it on his feed as proof of social practice.”

Another silence.

“All right,” said Uncle He. “I understand.”

“Uncle He.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t tell my dad.”

For a while there was no sound at the other end, only someone warbling away on the opera channel on the TV.

“Young master,” said Uncle He, “if the master knew about something like this, he’d handle it the same way.”

Ye Zhixing didn’t answer. He looked at the crossed-out word on the windowsill.

“…Don’t tell him yet.”

“All right.”

> Just went to the office to hand in homework and heard Mr. Sun’s been suspended??? People from the education bureau came  

The group exploded.

> ??? for real  
> why tho  
> is it the furniture thing  
> omg someone actually reported it  
> who was that brave  

Chen Xi posted a sticker in the group: a cat wearing sunglasses.

Ye Zhixing locked his phone, opened his chemistry book, copied the redox equation nobody had done onto scrap paper, and began to balance it.

## 6. Rice Noodles

The clay-pot rice noodle shop was at the other end of Back Street, next to a shoe-repair stall.

The shop was tiny, its frontage only two metres wide. On the glass door, in red cut-out vinyl, it said “Clay-pot rice noodles · Mini hotpot · Pick your own,” half the metal radical of one character missing. When you pushed the door open, a wave of heat smelling of chilli oil and bone broth hit you in the face; if you wore glasses, they fogged up instantly.

Inside were six small square tables, their tops covered in patterned plastic, a few spots burnt through by cigarette ends. On the wall hung an old television showing a costume drama, the volume turned very low; a woman was crying, crying without a sound.

Against the wall stood a row of chiller cabinets, their glass doors coated with white frost. Inside, compartment by compartment, were all kinds of things, each threaded on bamboo skewers, the end of each skewer painted a colour: red one yuan, yellow eighty fen, green fifty fen. Lamb rolls, beef rolls, fish balls, prawn balls, beef balls, pissing beef balls, fish tofu, crab sticks, luncheon meat, baby cabbage, lettuce, tofu skin, dried bean curd sticks, enoki, kelp knots, potato slices, lotus root slices… packed to the brim, the cold leaking out through the gaps in the glass doors and curling round your calves.

The owner was in her forties, wearing an apron printed with a cartoon pig, and the pig was laughing. She was cracking sunflower seeds behind the counter, and when she saw Abiao she didn’t even look up. “You lot again. No tabs today.”

“Who’s asking for a tab,” said Abiao. “Brother Xi’s treating us today.”

“When did I say I was treating?”

“Didn’t you just say you’re the best fighter round here?” said Abiao. “The best fighter not treating everyone, how would that look?”

Chubby and Beanpole doubled up laughing. The smallest one laughed along too, laughing so hard he nearly dropped his game controller into someone else’s pot.

Chen Xi swore, took his wallet out of his pocket, opened it, looked, and shut it again.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

They pushed two tables together and squeezed six people round them.

Each person had a small aluminium pot, with a little solid-fuel burner beneath it, its blue flame licking the bottom. The broth was the shop’s own, in three kinds: bone broth, tomato, and numbing-spicy. The owner said she fried her spicy base herself, a dozen-plus ingredients: beef tallow, ciba chilli, Sichuan pepper, star anise, black cardamom, bay leaves, and one thing brought from her home village, mountain pepper oil, which nobody else had.

The dipping-sauce bar was beside the chillers, a row of small stainless-steel bowls: minced garlic, coriander, spring onion, bird’s-eye chilli, sesame paste, oyster sauce, sesame oil, black vinegar, fermented tofu juice, crushed peanuts, and a big jar of the owner’s own chilli oil, with a thick layer of crisp-fried chilli flakes and sesame seeds sunk at the bottom, a layer of glossy red oil on top, a few black Sichuan peppercorns floating in it.

Abiao mixed a bowl of dipping sauce for everyone. He mixed with great care: two spoons of garlic, one of coriander, the chilli oil scooped together with the flakes underneath, and finally a ring of black vinegar on top.

“My secret recipe,” he said. “Everyone who tries it says it’s good.”

He set a bowl in front of Gu Xuerong.

“Can you eat spicy?”

Gu Xuerong looked at the bowl of fiery red sauce.

“…Yes.”

“Good,” said Abiao. “Doesn’t matter if you can’t, just dip less.”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Gu Xuerong sat at the far end, against the wall.

The little pot in front of her was bone broth; Chen Xi had ordered it for her. When he was choosing skewers he had asked what she wanted, she had said anything, and he had grabbed a handful from the chiller: two skewers of beef rolls, two of fish balls, one of baby cabbage, one of tofu skin, one of lotus root, and finally, after a moment’s thought, one of pissing beef balls.

The bone broth came to the boil, bubbling. A white broth with a few goji berries and two slices of ginger floating on top. She put the beef rolls in and watched them change colour bit by bit in the broth, from pink to greyish-white, their edges curling slightly.

Everyone else had already started eating.

Abiao ate the fiercest, one ball per mouthful, hissing at the heat, and still talking. He told them how last month in the internet café a middle-schooler had called him an “orphan,” and he hadn’t got angry, he had set the kid up on a machine and let him play all night. Beanpole said he actually was an orphan; Abiao said bollocks, my gran’s still alive; Beanpole said your gran brought you food just last week; Abiao said that’s because my gran loves me. Chubby laughed the whole time beside them, ear stud glinting, mouth too full of potato slices to speak.

The smallest one talked least. He kept his head down and ate. He ate fast, as if afraid someone would take it, chopsticks never stopping, cheeks bulging. Halfway through he looked up at Gu Xuerong, then at the few barely touched skewers in her bowl, and asked quietly, “Sis, aren’t you eating?”

Gu Xuerong looked at him.

There was still a bit of dust on his face, rubbed on when he was holding Gu Jianguo down. A patch behind his ear too.

She picked up a fish ball and put it in her mouth.

The fish ball was very hot. She held it in her mouth without chewing and waited for it to cool. The bone broth tasted plain: salty, with a little of the heat of the ginger. She bit into the fish ball; it was hollow, and a small gush of hot broth came out and scalded the tip of her tongue.

She ate one.

Then another.

She tried Abiao’s dipping sauce too. Garlic and vinegar hit first, then the heat, rising very slowly, inch by inch from the back of the tongue, and finally a fragrance she couldn’t name, a little like lemon and a little like fresh grass, that stayed in her mouth a long time.

“Well?” Abiao leaned over to ask.

“…It’s good.”

“Mountain pepper.” Abiao was very pleased with himself. “Told you.”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Chen Xi sat opposite her.

The corner of his mouth had stopped bleeding, leaving just a dark red scab. The punch to his stomach still hurt; every time he leaned forward to pick something out of the pot, his brows knitted. He ate very little, a few mouthfuls and then a stop, leaning back in his chair, watching the bone broth bubble.

He didn’t ask her what had just happened.

Nor why her father had cursed her, what those words meant, what was really going on in her family, or what she was going to do now.

He only, when the things in her bowl were nearly gone, got up and went to the chiller and brought back a few more skewers, and put them on her plate. One of luncheon meat, one of crab sticks, one of kelp knots.

“Eat more,” he said. “You’re too skinny, a breeze would blow you away.”

Gu Xuerong looked at the skewers.

“…On the day of military training, you said I had to apply for a fee waiver,” she said. “Lin Xiaoman told me.”

Chen Xi froze.

He opened his mouth, and his face slowly reddened, all the way to the roots of his ears.

“That—” He scratched the back of his head. “That day I was just running my mouth. I was just… talking rubbish. I didn’t know you really were…”

He didn’t finish. He lowered his head and stirred his chopsticks around in the pot, stirring for ages without picking anything up.

“Sorry,” he said.

So quietly it was almost drowned out by the bubbling of the pot.

She reached out with her chopsticks, took a piece of luncheon meat from the skewers he had pushed over, and put it in her mouth.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

When it came to paying, the six of them had eaten a hundred and thirty-seven yuan’s worth.

Chen Xi took out his wallet. There was a hundred and five yuan in it: one fifty, two twenties, one ten, one five. He took it all out and held it in his hand, and his face went red again.

Abiao fished a crumpled twenty out of his pocket, screwed into a ball, and tossed it on the counter. Beanpole produced ten, Chubby two coins, and the smallest one searched every pocket he had for ages and came up with a handful of ten- and fifty-fen pieces; he counted them: one yuan seventy.

Still a little short.

Gu Xuerong reached into her schoolbag.

“Don’t.” Chen Xi pressed down on her wrist.

It was her left wrist he pressed, through the sleeve of her school jacket. He didn’t press hard, but her whole arm went rigid at once, as if something had stung it. Chen Xi felt it, let go immediately and drew back a little.

“…I said I’m paying,” he said. “Don’t you move.”

Behind the counter, the owner watched this crowd for a while, then gathered the pile of money towards her and counted it.

“A hundred and thirty-two seventy,” she said. “Call it done.”

“You’re knocking off five?”

“Call it done.” The owner picked up her sunflower seeds again. “Bring more people next time. Business is slow.”

## 7. Catching Up on Sleep

Gu Xuerong got back to the dormitory a little after one in the afternoon.

There was nobody in the room. Lin Xiaoman was still in class, and so were the other two girls. The room was so quiet you could hear someone downstairs chopping something, thud, thud, thud, one blow after another, very rhythmic. The four girls’ washing on the balcony swayed slightly in the wind, and its shadows on the floor swayed with it.

Lin Xiaoman’s bunk was a mess, the quilt balled up, an open comic by the pillow, half a packet of crisps lying on its pages.

On the little table by Gu Xuerong’s bed sat the pink insulated lunchbox. On its cloth cover, the rabbits were smiling.

She went over, picked up the lunchbox and opened the lid.

It was empty. Washed very clean, a few drops of water still inside.

Under the lunchbox was a sticky note in Lin Xiaoman’s handwriting, round and bubbly, like a string of bubbles:

> My fever went this lunchtime!! I’ll get your dinner tonight!! What do you want?? (You’re NOT allowed to say anything)  

After it she had drawn a crying face, then a smiling face, the two faces side by side as if they were arguing.

Gu Xuerong read the “no saying ‘whatever’” twice.

She peeled it off, folded it in half and put it in the pocket of her school jacket.

Then she lay down.

She didn’t take off her uniform or her shoes. She just lay on her side on the bed, facing the wall. There was a water stain on the wall shaped like a crouching rabbit; she had noticed it long ago and never told anyone.

Her hand went into her sleeve and found her left wrist. It didn’t move; she just rested her hand there, pressed against it.

The sliver of sky outside the window was white. The sun was behind the clouds, and the light was diffuse, coming in through the window onto the floor, onto the edge of the bed, without a single shadow.

She closed her eyes.

Downstairs, the chopping stopped.

She fell asleep.

She didn’t dream.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

When she woke it was twenty past four in the afternoon.

The light outside had changed colour, from white to a very pale gold, slanting in through the window and cutting across her face. She squinted at the beam for a while, at the dust floating in it, mote by mote, slowly turning.

She got up and washed her face.

The water from the tap was cold. She cupped her hands and splashed her face twice, then left her hands in the water a while longer, until her fingertips were cold right through, before turning it off.

The face in the mirror was still white, but not as white as that morning. The two blue patches under her eyes were still there, but her lips had a little colour now, not much, like a watercolour brush lightly touched to wet paper.

She changed her hair tie and tied her hair up again.

As she went out, she took the folded sticky note out of her pocket, looked at it once more, and put it back.

## 8. The Second Floor

The street lights on Back Street weren’t on yet.

The copier in the copy shop was still running. The owner was sitting on a little stool at the door; seeing her, she smiled and waved. “Xuerong, you’re here. It’s busy up there.”

She went upstairs.

The stairs were wooden, twenty-one in all, and she counted every one. At the fifteenth she smelled pickled cabbage and beef drifting down from above, mixed with a hint of curry.

She pushed the door open.

Su Tang was crouched under the windowsill combing the Ragdoll. The Ragdoll was swearing and Su Tang was swearing back, keeping her voice low: “Your Highness, one more word out of you today and you can forget about treats, Your Highness.” In the open space by the window three middle-schoolers lay on their stomachs with feather wands, the calico turning somersaults between them. Behind the kitchen’s quilted curtain Old Zhou’s griddle was sizzling, and he was humming a song, the same one, still out of tune.

On the grey sofa against the wall sat Ye Zhixing.

On the big screen in front of him was Nightmare Raid’s login screen: the rainy corridor, the half-open door at the end, the bit of red light leaking through the gap. He had a controller in his hands but wasn’t playing, just holding it, looking at the screen.

He heard the door and turned his head.

When he saw it was her, his fingers moved on the controller.

“You’re here.”

“Mm.”

She walked over and sat down beside him. The sofa springs creaked.

He handed her the other controller. She took it; it was warm, from being held for a long time.

Neither of them mentioned what had happened that day.

He didn’t ask what her father had said after he came, didn’t ask what had happened at the corner of Back Street, didn’t ask whether she was all right, didn’t ask whether she was going back to the dormitory tonight. She didn’t ask him what had happened with Mr. Sun, didn’t ask what Chen Xi had told him, didn’t ask where he had gone after he walked out of chemistry that morning.

On the screen, the rainy corridor began to stretch ahead.

“Left or right?” he asked.

“Right.”

“Last time you said right, something dropped from the ceiling.”

“Not this time.”

“How do you know?”

“I know.”

So he went right.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

In the third round, Su Tang came running over from the windowsill with a receipt in her hand.

“Xuerong, that table just now, two curries and a lemon tea, QR, thirty-six.”

Gu Xuerong put her controller on her knees, picked up the ledger from the arm of the sofa, opened it to today’s page, picked up her pen and wrote it down.

Time, four fifty-one. Two curry beef rice, one lemon tea, QR, thirty-six yuan.

Her writing was still very small, but every stroke was steady. The loop of the 6 was drawn perfectly round.

She put the ledger back on the arm of the sofa and picked up her controller again.

On the screen, Ye Zhixing’s character stood in the middle of the corridor, not moving, waiting for her.

“Why aren’t you going?”

“Waiting for you.”

“…Let’s go.”

The two characters walked on together. At the first corner a hand reached out of the wallpaper; Ye Zhixing dodged right and got past it. He was a little pleased with himself and had just turned his head to say something when the screen went dark—something dropped from the ceiling and swallowed his character whole.

“…Didn’t you say not this time?”

“I said I wouldn’t.”

Her character stood beside the spot where his had fallen, and didn’t go on. She waited for him to respawn.

Ye Zhixing turned to look at her. She was watching the screen, the corner of her mouth turned up a little, a very little, as if something had floated up from under the water, touched the surface lightly, and sunk again.

He looked for a while, then turned back and went on playing.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

A little after six, Chen Xi sent a message.

> she ate two fish balls a beef ball a piece of luncheon meat a skewer of kelp and half a skewer of beef  

Ye Zhixing looked at the message for a while.

He replied:

> thanks  

And added:

> put iodine on your lip  

Chen Xi sent a sticker: a cat wearing sunglasses.

Ye Zhixing put his phone face down on the arm of the sofa.

Beside him, Gu Xuerong was doing the accounts again. Su Tang called out a sale, and she wrote it down. Outside the window the street lights came on one after another, and the plane leaves under them were so yellow they were translucent. Old Zhou’s griddle was still sizzling, and the Ragdoll was still swearing.

She finished the entry, put the cap on her pen, slid it back into the spine of the ledger, and picked up her controller again.

“Again,” she said.

# Chapter Nine　A Bit More Normal

## 1. What She Plays

Su Tang asked on a Tuesday evening.

It was raining that day and the shop was quiet; only two groups came in, ate, fussed over the cats for a while and left. The rain had started at three in the afternoon. It wasn’t heavy, just fine and steady, hitting the second-floor windows and running down them in streaks, soaking the row of plane trees outside into a yellow blur. Inside, the warm lights were on and the cats were all drowsy. Rice Cake had curled up on the windowsill with its back to the rain, sound asleep; the calico was squeezed up against the Devon, whose big ears twitched now and then, dreaming.

Old Zhou was in the kitchen scrubbing griddle plates. Sister Mei had taken the day off; her child had a fever.

Su Tang finished combing the last cat, picked the fur out of the comb bit by bit and put it back in her canvas bag, then sat down at the other end of the sofa, hugging her knees, and looked at Gu Xuerong.

Gu Xuerong was looking at her phone. The light of the screen fell on her face and turned her already pale face bluish. She was very absorbed, barely blinking, now and then swiping a finger across the screen.

“Xuerong.”

“Mm.”

“What do you usually play?”

Gu Xuerong’s finger paused.

“…Games.”

“What games?” Su Tang shuffled closer. “The one you always play with Ye Zhixing, the rainy corridor one, I know that. What else? What do you play when you’re on your own?”

Gu Xuerong didn’t answer right away. She raised her eyes, past Su Tang, to behind the counter.

Ye Zhixing was sitting behind the counter checking delivery slips. At this he looked up.

He looked at Su Tang, then at Gu Xuerong, and put down the slips.

“Su Tang.”

“Hm?”

“Have you had dinner?”

“Yes, Old Zhou made me an omelette rice.”

“How long ago?”

Su Tang paused. “…An hour or so? Why?”

Ye Zhixing didn’t answer. He turned to Gu Xuerong. She was looking at him too, her expression the same as ever, flat, giving nothing away, but the hand holding the phone drew back a little, as if waiting to see what he meant.

“The stuff she plays,” said Ye Zhixing, choosing his words, “isn’t really… suitable after a meal.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean,” he thought for a moment, “if you want to look, don’t face the screen straight on. Keep it a bit away. If it feels wrong, close your eyes.”

Su Tang looked at him, then at Gu Xuerong, and her expression grew suspicious bit by bit, and then, bit by bit, excited. The kind of excitement a child gets on hearing that a certain room is off limits.

“Is it really that bad?”

“Yes.”

“I’ve watched horror films,” said Su Tang. “I’ve even watched The Grudge.”

Ye Zhixing thought of that night. The glow of the monitor, the blue night light in the corner of the aquarium, the cold floor tiles, the hum of the bathroom extractor fan.

“…That’s different,” he said.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Gu Xuerong said nothing. She turned her phone round and handed it to Su Tang.

On the screen was a folder with a dozen or so icons lined up in it, all of them dark: red, black, brown. Some showed an iron door, some a cross, some nothing at all, just an indistinct mass.

Su Tang’s finger hovered over the screen for a while.

“What’s this one?” She pointed at the first.

“Lucifer’s Dungeon.”

“And this?”

“The Passion. Not the film. A game.”

“This one?”

“Escape from the Ghost Farm.”

Su Tang took a breath and opened the first one.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Ye Zhixing didn’t watch the screen. He watched Su Tang’s face.

At first she was smiling, with a hint of challenge, the corners of her mouth turned up, as if to say: is that all? The light of the screen changed colour on her face: dark red first, then black, then a very bright, glaring white.

Then her smile stopped.

Not all at once. Slowly, starting at the corners of her mouth, drawing back bit by bit, like a tide going out. Her eyes went wide, her brows rose and then knotted, and finally her whole face screwed up into a knot.

A sound came out of the phone. Very low, very wet, like something being slowly wrung.

Su Tang flung the phone onto the sofa and clapped a hand over her mouth.

She stood up, too fast; her knee hit the little round table, a paper cup tipped over and lemon tea spilled across the table. She didn’t care. Hand over her mouth, she ran towards the kitchen, changed direction halfway and made for the sink by the back-room door.

Then came a very loud sound.

Ye Zhixing closed his eyes for a moment.

The kitchen’s quilted curtain lifted and Old Zhou looked out, steel wool still in hand. “What happened, what happened?”

“Nothing,” said Ye Zhixing. “She saw something.”

Old Zhou looked at Su Tang bent over the sink, then at Gu Xuerong on the sofa and the phone lying face down on the sofa cushion. He asked nothing, turned and went back into the kitchen, and after a while came out with a glass of warm water, put it on the counter by the sink, and went back in.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Gu Xuerong got up from the sofa.

She went over to the sink, not too close, and stopped behind Su Tang. Su Tang was still bent over, both hands braced on the edge of the sink, her shoulders heaving, her bun knocked to one side, a few loose strands stuck to her neck with sweat.

Gu Xuerong picked up the glass of water Old Zhou had left and held it out.

Su Tang took it, rinsed her mouth, drank two mouthfuls, caught her breath and turned to look at her. Her eyes were red, tears hanging on her lashes, half from being sick and half from fright.

“You…” Su Tang’s voice was hoarse. “This is what you usually play?”

“Yes.”

“On your own? At night?”

“Yes.”

“Aren’t you scared?”

Gu Xuerong thought about it.

She seemed to really be thinking. Her eyes moved to one side and came to rest on what was still in the sink, waiting to be rinsed away, stayed there a while, and came back.

“What does scared mean?” she said.

Su Tang was thrown. “…Scared, you know. Your heart going thump thump, your legs going weak, not daring to go forward, that kind of thing.”

Gu Xuerong thought a while longer. The rain was still falling, pattering on the window. In the kitchen Old Zhou was stacking the griddle plates one on another, iron knocking on iron, ting, ting.

“I don’t know what frightening is.”

When she had said it she turned and went back to the sofa, picked up the phone lying face down there, locked it and put it in the pocket of her school jacket. Then she took a stack of tissues and went to wipe up the spilled lemon tea on the little round table.

Su Tang stood by the sink watching her back, and didn’t notice she had crushed the empty paper cup in her hand.

## 2. Patches

That night after closing, Su Tang didn’t leave straight away.

Uncle Chen’s car was already at the mouth of the alley. She rang him and said she needed ten more minutes. Then she stood by the counter and watched Ye Zhixing lock the drawer, put away the payment code, and switch off the big screen at the wall. Gu Xuerong had already gone; before leaving she had put the ledger in the drawer and the pen back in the pen pot, nib down.

“Ye Zhixing.”

“Mm.”

“Those games,” said Su Tang. “Can you buy them?”

Ye Zhixing’s hand paused on the drawer lock.

“…No,” he said. “Not in China. The ones that exist abroad won’t sell to minors, you have to verify your ID. Some were never put on sale at all, people made them themselves and put them online, you need a password, an invitation, you have to get through several layers.”

“Then how did she get them?”

He had seen that folder of hers. Not today; the week before, she had been installing a game on the shop computer and halfway through asked him to look at an error. He had leaned over to look, and what he saw wasn’t an ordinary installer but a window of white text on black, lines of it scrolling past.

She had got round that game’s age verification. Not with a tool someone else had written: she had modified it herself. She had found the section that did the verification, cut it out, and patched the gap she had cut, patched it so seamlessly the game itself couldn’t tell. The folder held a dozen more things like that, each followed by a small text file named with a date, recording what she had changed, where she had got stuck, and how she had got round it.

Those notes were very detailed, more detailed than the accounts she kept.

At the time he had looked at that window for a long time without saying anything. She thought he didn’t understand it and pointed at one line: “It errors here.” He said, “Yeah, you’re missing a semicolon here,” and she went and added a semicolon, and the game installed.

“She did it herself,” said Ye Zhixing.

“Herself?”

“Yes.”

Su Tang stood there with the strap of her canvas bag twisted into a knot in her hand.

“She’s only sixteen,” said Su Tang.

“I know.”

“She’s so…” Su Tang looked for a word and didn’t find one. “She can’t even keep the accounts straight, she’s always writing the numbers wrong, and she can do this by herself?”

Ye Zhixing switched off the last light. The room went dark, with only a little light from the street lamps outside coming in, filtered through the forest-green curtains into a very dim green.

“She’s not stupid,” he said.

He said that, and didn’t go on. Su Tang waited a while, and nothing more came.

“Then she needs to be a bit more normal,” said Su Tang.

Ye Zhixing looked at her.

“I mean,” Su Tang’s voice dropped, “I don’t mean she’s not normal. I mean… she can’t play that stuff on her own every night. Till two or three in the morning. People break doing that.”

When she said “break,” her voice shook slightly.

Outside, an electric scooter went past, its headlight sweeping across the ceiling from one end to the other.

“I’ve got loads of normal stuff,” said Su Tang. “Anime, games, I’ve got a whole hard drive at home. I’ll bring it tomorrow.”

“She might not play them.”

“Then help me persuade her.”

“…I have tried.”

Su Tang looked at him.

“Then try again,” she said.

## 3. Normal Stuff

The next day Su Tang really did bring a hard drive.

A black portable hard drive in a pink silicone case covered in stickers: cats, rabbits, a duck wearing a crown. She set it down on the little round table in front of Gu Xuerong as if handing over a very important document.

“Everything in here,” she said, “is normal.”

Gu Xuerong looked down at the drive for a while, then up at Su Tang.

“What counts as normal?”

Su Tang opened her mouth.

“…Like,” she said, “stuff that won’t make you throw up.”

Gu Xuerong thought about it. “The one who threw up was Ye Zhixing, not me.”

Su Tang turned her head and stared hard at Ye Zhixing. Ye Zhixing, behind the counter, pretended to be looking at his phone. After three seconds of being stared at, he sighed and put the phone down.

“Try it,” he said. “Just try it. If it’s no fun, don’t play.”

Gu Xuerong looked at him for a while.

That while went on a bit long. Long enough that Su Tang thought she was going to refuse, and her fingers had started twisting the bag strap.

“…Okay.”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

The first was Overcooked.

Su Tang chose it. She said it was the simplest: four people cooking together, chopping, making soup, serving plates, washing up, too much for one person, so everyone had to work together. She roped in Ye Zhixing, and then fetched Uncle He up from downstairs, where he was chatting with the copy-shop owner. Uncle He said he didn’t know how to play; Su Tang said never mind, just stand there and wash up.

Four people, four controllers, squeezed onto the grey sofa under the big screen.

Level one was onion soup.

Su Tang chopped onions, Ye Zhixing made soup, Uncle He washed up—he really did just stand at the sink washing up, gripping his controller tight, eyes narrowed, as serious as if he were checking a ledger—and Gu Xuerong was in charge of serving.

It started all right.

In the second round, three orders popped up on screen at once. Su Tang shouted, “Xuerong, plates!” Gu Xuerong’s character stood in the kitchen holding an empty plate for two seconds, then turned and walked off the other way, to a corner nobody had noticed, where there was a stove with nothing on it.

She stood in front of that stove and stopped.

“Xuerong, what are you doing over there?”

“There’s a stove here.”

“That stove’s no use, you don’t need that stove—”

Gu Xuerong’s character put the plate in her hands on that stove.

The stove caught fire.

The plate caught fire.

The fire started in that corner and spread along the counters, reaching Ye Zhixing’s soup pot, reaching Su Tang’s chopping board, reaching Uncle He’s sink. The whole kitchen was ablaze. Four little figures ran around in the flames, and a huge red word jumped up on the screen: FAILED.

Su Tang stared at the screen.

Uncle He was still gripping his controller. His expression didn’t change; he just blinked once.

Ye Zhixing turned to look at Gu Xuerong.

Gu Xuerong looked at the fire on the screen for a while.

“…It looks nice when it burns,” she said.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

They played a few more levels after that.

Gu Xuerong wasn’t stupid. The more Ye Zhixing watched, the surer of it he was. Her hands were quick, quicker than Su Tang’s, quicker than his, her button rhythm steady and precise when she chopped. Her problem wasn’t her hands. It was direction.

She always went off to do what nobody else was doing.

When everyone was chopping, she went to mop the floor; when everyone was serving, she went to investigate that stove nobody would ever use; when the orders were on the left, she walked to the right, to the edge of the map, and stood there looking at the part nobody else went to. She wasn’t messing about on purpose. She genuinely thought that side mattered more, or looked nicer, or—Ye Zhixing couldn’t say quite what—it was more like an instinct, like water running downhill: she always headed for where there was nobody.

“Xuerong,” said Su Tang, by level five finally unable to hold it in, “can’t you just go where everyone else goes?”

“Why?”

“Because we’re a team!”

Gu Xuerong didn’t answer. Her character stood in a small corner at the edge of the map. In that corner was a window, and outside it was the game’s painted sea, blue, perfectly still.

After a while her character turned round, walked slowly back into the kitchen, and picked up a plate.

That level, they got one star.

Su Tang was so pleased she bounced on the sofa, nearly knocking Uncle He’s controller out of his hands. Uncle He put the controller down, rubbed his eyes, said he was getting old and his eyes couldn’t keep up, stood up and went downstairs with his hands behind his back. At the door he turned and said, “Playing again tomorrow?”

Su Tang said yes.

Uncle He nodded and went down.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

The second was Stardew Valley.

This time Ye Zhixing chose. He said you could play it alone or together, no need to coordinate: farming, keeping chickens, fishing, mining, do whatever you like, nobody hurries you.

Gu Xuerong played for an hour.

The first thing she did when the game started was go mining.

Ye Zhixing watched her character dig down level after level, to the tenth, the twentieth, her health bar getting shorter, her backpack crammed with stone and copper ore. She didn’t go back to farm, didn’t go into town to talk to anyone. She just kept digging down, one level, then another.

“Aren’t you going to farm?”

“I did.”

Ye Zhixing switched to her farm to look. In the ground were a row of parsnips, five of them, planted in the farthest corner of the farm, a long way from the house, surrounded by weeds and rocks. Five parsnips in a row, very neat, like a line of small writing.

“Just five?”

“That’s enough.”

“…There’s a huge patch of land right outside your house. Why plant them in that corner?”

“It’s quiet there.”

Ye Zhixing looked at the five parsnips for a while and asked nothing more.

That night she dug down to the fortieth level of the mine, fell into a hole and passed out. When she came to, half the money in her wallet was gone and several things were missing from her backpack.

She looked at the line on the screen: “You passed out in the mines.”

“…Not bad,” she said.

Su Tang was about to say something again; under the sofa, Ye Zhixing nudged her shoe with the toe of his. Su Tang glanced at him and swallowed it.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

The anime Su Tang picked out one by one.

She had made a folder on the hard drive called “For Xuerong,” with seven or eight series in it. Natsume’s Book of Friends, Laid-Back Camp, K-On!, Shirobako, and a few long-titled slice-of-life shows that were her own favourites. After each file name she had added a note in brackets:

> Natsume’s Book of Friends (yokai but really gentle!! not scary!!)  
> Laid-Back Camp (just some girls going camping, really comfy to watch)  
> K-On! (they play music, then drink tea, then play music)  

Gu Xuerong read the brackets one by one, and at “then drink tea, then play music,” the corner of her mouth moved.

“I don’t watch things at the shop,” she said.

“Then watch them back home,” said Su Tang. “Back in the dormitory. Copy them onto your phone and watch these when you can’t sleep. Don’t watch that other stuff.”

Gu Xuerong neither agreed nor refused.

She copied the folder onto her phone. While it copied, Su Tang stood beside her watching the progress bar, and only when it reached a hundred per cent did she let out a breath, like someone who had escorted something all the way to its destination.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

That night Lin Xiaoman was doing practice problems in the dormitory. A bit after eleven she looked down at the lower bunk.

Gu Xuerong was lying on her side, facing the wall, her phone held up in front of her. The light of the screen fell on the wall in a small bright square.

Lin Xiaoman assumed she was playing the rainy-corridor game again. She craned her neck and looked down.

On the screen was a boy in glasses sitting in a very green meadow, and crouched beside him a round, white cat that looked like a lucky-cat figurine. Wind passed over the meadow, the grass bending in waves and standing up again. The boy was talking to the cat, softly, slowly, and the music was a very simple piano line, ting, ting, ting.

Lin Xiaoman watched for a while, said nothing, pulled her head back, and went on with her problems.

Two problems later, she leaned out to look again.

Gu Xuerong was still watching. The white cat seemed to have said something funny, and the boy laughed. The light of the screen flickered on the wall.

Lin Xiaoman didn’t know whether Gu Xuerong was laughing along. From where she was, she could only see the back of Gu Xuerong’s head and that tiny black bun.

She turned her desk lamp down a little and went on with her problems.

## 4. A Thousand Yuan

Chen Xi got the money on a Friday afternoon.

Ninth period had just ended. He was swinging his bag onto his shoulder, about to go to the internet café on Back Street to find Abiao, when his phone buzzed.

It was a transfer.

> Ye Zhixing transferred ¥1,000.00 to you  

Followed by a line:

> For the other day  

Chen Xi stood at the classroom door staring at the number. He held the phone closer, then further away, and counted the zeros.

Three zeros.

He had been at No. 8 High for just over two months and hanging around Back Street for three years, and the most money he had ever held in his life was last New Year’s lucky money from his uncle, six hundred yuan, which his mum took the next day, saying she’d keep it safe for him. He still hadn’t seen it since.

He put the phone in his pocket, turned and walked back into the classroom.

Ye Zhixing was still at his desk packing up, his bag half zipped. Chen Xi went over, stopped by his desk, took out his phone and held the screen towards him.

“Brother Ye, this…”

“Keep it.”

“It’s too much.”

“It’s not much. That punch you took was worth it.”

“I just…” Chen Xi scratched the back of his head, his face slowly reddening. “That day I just didn’t like the look of him, I wasn’t doing it for—”

“I know.” Ye Zhixing zipped his bag. “That’s why I’m giving it to you.”

Chen Xi stood there, mouth open.

“The scar on your lip hasn’t healed yet,” said Ye Zhixing. “And your friends, they all piled in that day too. Split it, take them for a proper meal. Not that rice-noodle place. Somewhere expensive.”

He shouldered his bag, walked past Chen Xi to the back door, and turned round.

“Don’t tell anyone.”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Chen Xi didn’t tell anyone, apart from Abiao and the others.

That night, on the long sofa at the very back of the internet café, he split the thousand yuan five ways. Two hundred for himself, and two hundred each for Abiao, Beanpole, Chubby and the smallest one. He sent it by transfer, one at a time, and when he had finished he posted a line in their five-person group chat:

> from brother ye, says thanks everyone for helping that day  

The group was quiet for about a minute.

Then Abiao sent a string of exclamation marks. Beanpole sent a “?”, then a “!”, then another “?”. Chubby sent a sticker of a panda on its knees kowtowing. The smallest one sent nothing, and after a long while messaged Chen Xi privately:

> brother xi who is this brother ye  

Chen Xi thought about it and replied:

> the big boss  

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

From then on, in class Chen Xi called Ye Zhixing “Brother Ye,” and on Back Street he called him “Boss.”

The first time Ye Zhixing heard him say “Boss” was outside the internet café on Back Street. He had come down from the cat café and was heading to the mouth of the alley to wait for Uncle Chen when he ran into Chen Xi and Abiao crouched outside the café eating grilled sausages. Chen Xi saw him and shot to his feet, sausage still in his mouth, and called out indistinctly, “Boss!”

Abiao stood up too. Beanpole and Chubby poked their heads out of the café, saw who it was, and stood up as well. The four of them lined up outside the internet café like a row of soldiers waiting for inspection.

Ye Zhixing stood there and looked at them for two seconds.

“…Don’t call me that. Sounds like you’re collecting protection money.”

“Then what do we call you?”

“My name.”

“No way.” Chen Xi took the sausage out of his mouth and said, very seriously, “Using your name isn’t respectful.”

“Was it respectful back when you called me Young Master Ye?”

Chen Xi’s face went red at once. Abiao laughed so hard he dropped his sausage.

Ye Zhixing said nothing more and walked off towards the mouth of the alley. Halfway there he heard Chen Xi behind him talking to Abiao, voice lowered, though not low enough:

“…I’m telling you, this guy’s loyal. He didn’t give us money because he’s rich, he gave it because he felt he owed us. Get it? Someone like that, you’re good to him, he’s good to you for life.”

“How do you know?”

“I’m a good judge of people.”

Ye Zhixing didn’t look back.

He reached the mouth of the alley. Uncle Chen’s car was there, headlights on. He opened the door, got in, leaned back in his seat and closed his eyes for a while.

“Young master,” said Uncle Chen, glancing at him in the rear-view mirror, “what are you smiling about?”

“I’m not smiling.”

Uncle Chen asked nothing more and started the car.

## 5. Midterms

The midterm exams were in the first week of November.

Three days of them. Chinese, maths, English, physics, chemistry, biology, politics, history, geography: nine subjects, one paper each, set by the year office for the whole year and printed on the duplicator in the academic office, yellow paper, blue ink, with a heavy smell of printing ink.

The results came out on the Monday of the following week.

The year rankings were pinned up on the noticeboard in the ground-floor hall of the teaching block: three big white sheets, ranked top to bottom, more than five hundred names. The crowd in front of the noticeboard was packed solid, people at the front looking for their names, people at the back pushing forward, some on tiptoe, some riding on classmates’ shoulders.

Ye Zhixing didn’t push in. He stood outside the crowd, leaning against a pillar, waiting for it to thin out.

Suddenly someone in the crowd shouted:

“—What the hell! Chen Xi’s second??”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

That shout was like a stone thrown into water. The crowd erupted.

“Chen Xi? Which Chen Xi?”

“Chen Xi from Class Seven! The one who skips every day!”

“No way. He copied, right?”

“Copied who? There’s only one person above him. He copied the person in first place? Who’s first?”

“…Ye Zhixing.”

“Then he copied Ye Zhixing! Aren’t they in the same class?”

“Different exam rooms, though. Ye Zhixing was in Room One, Chen Xi was in… Chen Xi was in Room Twelve.”

“Room Twelve’s a whole building away from Room One.”

The crowd went quiet for a moment.

“Then how did he do it?”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Chen Xi himself heard the news in the internet café.

Abiao came over holding his phone and shoved the photo from the class group chat in his face: the big white sheet on the noticeboard, first line “Ye Zhixing, Class 7, 836,” second line “Chen Xi, Class 7, 812,” third line a girl from Class Three next door, “781,” thirty-one points below him.

Chen Xi glanced at it, said “Huh,” and went on playing.

“Huh?” Abiao glared at him. “That’s it, ‘huh’?”

“What else?”

“You’re fucking second! Second in the whole year! You hang out here with us every day and you’re fucking second!”

“I was second in middle school,” said Chen Xi. “In the high school entrance exam too. The one ahead of me went to a school in the city. I didn’t.”

Abiao’s mouth hung open for ages.

“…Why didn’t you go?”

Chen Xi kept his eyes on the screen, fingers never stopping on the keyboard.

“Couldn’t afford it,” he said.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Ye Zhixing learned Chen Xi’s scores from the new homeroom teacher.

The new homeroom teacher was called Zheng, in her early thirties, and taught English; she had moved over from Year Two after Mr. Sun was suspended. She was small and softly spoken, wore round glasses, and the first time she stood at the lectern and people were talking, she didn’t shout. She just stood there and waited until the classroom went quiet by itself.

The day the results came out, she called Chen Xi to her office.

Ye Zhixing went to the office to hand in homework and happened to hear it from the doorway.

“Chen Xi,” said Ms. Zheng, her voice gentle, “you got a hundred and forty-eight in maths, a hundred in physics, ninety-eight in chemistry. A hundred and forty-one in English.” She paused. “You don’t seem to… listen much in class?”

“Not much,” said Chen Xi.

“Then how did you learn it?”

“Reading.”

“Reading what?”

“The textbook,” said Chen Xi. “It’s all written in the textbook.”

Ms. Zheng was silent for a while. The two other teachers in the office had stopped what they were doing and were looking over.

“And your Chinese…” Ms. Zheng turned to another paper. “A hundred and three. Twenty off for reading comprehension, eighteen off for the essay.”

“Mm.”

“What did you write your essay about?”

Chen Xi scratched his head. “The title was ‘The person I’ll never forget.’”

“Yes.”

“I wrote about my gran’s dog.”

The office went quiet for a moment.

“…A dog?”

“It’s the one I’ll never forget,” said Chen Xi. “It pulled me out of the river with its teeth once. When I was eight. Later someone poisoned it and hung it from the tree at the edge of the village. That’s what I wrote.”

Ms. Zheng looked down and read the essay through again from the beginning.

“It’s not bad,” she said, her voice quieter still. “It’s just… too short. The requirement was six hundred characters, and you wrote three hundred and twenty.”

“When it’s finished, it’s finished,” said Chen Xi. “There wasn’t anything else worth writing.”

Ms. Zheng looked up at him. She said nothing, and after a while folded the paper and handed it back to him.

“Next time,” she said, “write enough words.”

“…Okay.”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Ye Zhixing put his homework on the desk by the door, turned and left.

He didn’t tell Chen Xi he had heard.

But after that he looked at Chen Xi in class a little differently. Chen Xi was still Chen Xi: asleep in lessons, stirring things up between them, a loose mouth, always ready with a comeback, able to chat with anyone, out the back door the moment ninth period began. But when he slipped out, there was always a textbook stuffed in his bag, his own, the corners of its pages curled and fuzzy from turning.

Once Ye Zhixing caught a glimpse inside that book. A physics textbook, every blank space covered in writing, dense, not notes but formulas he had derived himself, page after page, carried a long way, carried on to places the textbook didn’t go.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

As for everyone else, they weren’t so lucky.

Su Tang came forty-seventh in the year. She was in Class Three, and Class Three’s homeroom teacher praised her at the class meeting for the big improvement. She came back to the cat café bouncing about and told everyone, then got a bit embarrassed and said it wasn’t really that good, only top fifty.

Lin Xiaoman came four hundred and twenty-first. When she saw her score she sighed, said it was twenty points up on last time, that was progress, and she’d have an extra chicken leg tonight to celebrate.

Gu Xuerong’s name was on the third big white sheet.

Very far down, seven or eight lines from the bottom of the sheet.

She didn’t go to look. Lin Xiaoman looked for her, and when she came back she didn’t tell her the ranking, just said “Exams are over, that’s the main thing, don’t think about them now,” and pushed the lunchbox towards her, saying there were braised pork ribs today.

Gu Xuerong didn’t ask either.

## 6. Lunch

What made Ye Zhixing notice was a plastic bag.

It was a Wednesday lunch break, and he was coming back from the canteen past Gu Xuerong’s desk. She was asleep on it, forehead against her arm, her right hand gripping her left cuff. A plastic bag was stuffed in her desk, its mouth open, and inside was a bun, unopened, the use-by date printed on its wrapper already two days gone.

He thought for a moment, and then other things came back to him.

That she was never in the canteen in the mornings. That her face was always at its whitest in first period, white to the point of blue, and whiter still by third and fourth, her lips colourless. That once in PE, running the 800 metres, she had stopped on the second lap and held on to the railing at the edge of the track for a long time; when the PE teacher went over to ask, she said she was fine, and after a while she walked slowly back to the line on her own.

That she had once said something to him. Late one night in the shop he had asked what time she went to sleep, and she said three; he asked what time she got up, and she said ten past seven; he asked what about breakfast, and she said she didn’t eat it; he asked what about lunch, and she said at lunchtime she was sleepy, so she slept.

At the time he hadn’t taken it to heart.

Now he did.

No. 8 High let out at half past five, the canteen served dinner at six, and after six there were four more evening lessons. Every day at six, Lin Xiaoman got the food from the canteen, ran all the way to the dormitory with it in the little gap before evening lessons began, put it by Gu Xuerong’s bed, and ran all the way back, often making it into the classroom just as the bell rang. The two of them didn’t actually say much to each other most of the time, but Lin Xiaoman had never missed a single day with that lunchbox.

That was all Gu Xuerong ate each day, that one meal. At nine-something, ten, she got back from the shop and opened the insulated lunchbox; the food had long since stopped being very warm, and she ate half of it, sometimes a third.

One day, just that much.

He stood by her desk looking down at the out-of-date bun, and stayed there a good while.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

That evening he found Su Tang at the shop.

Su Tang was blow-drying the Devon after its bath. The hairdryer droned, and the Devon huddled in her arms, big ears flat against its head, looking as if it had lost the will to live.

“Su Tang.”

“Hm?” Su Tang switched off the dryer. “What’s up?”

“At your lunch break, can you leave the school?”

“Yes,” said Su Tang. “Twelve to half past one, you can go out to eat, as long as you’re back before half one. Why?”

Ye Zhixing glanced over at the sofa. Gu Xuerong was sitting there with the ledger open on her knees, going through the day’s menu with Old Zhou. Old Zhou said an item and she wrote it down, writing very slowly.

“Every lunchtime,” said Ye Zhixing, lowering his voice, “take a meal from the shop and give it to her.”

Su Tang followed his gaze over, then turned back.

“…Xuerong?”

“Yes.”

“She doesn’t eat breakfast?”

“No. Or lunch.”

Su Tang’s brows drew together. She looked down at the Devon in her arms, its fur still damp, in strands. She stroked its back, smoothing it several times.

“I did think,” she said, “how did she get so thin.”

“I’ll talk to Old Zhou. He makes one portion every lunchtime, you come and get it at twelve and take it to her at school,” said Ye Zhixing. “I’ll pay for the food, and the trip is paid separately.”

“No need to pay me separately.”

“Separately.”

Su Tang looked at him for a while.

“Why don’t you give it to her yourself?”

“If I give it to her, she’ll say ‘I’ll pay you back,’” he said. “Then she’ll put it in her desk to keep the bun company till it grows fur.”

“If you give it to her, she’s got nothing to say.”

Su Tang looked at him a while longer, then lowered her head and switched the hairdryer back on.

“Okay,” she said, half drowned out by the dryer. “I’ll give it to her.”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

At ten past twelve the next day.

Gu Xuerong was lying on her desk. There weren’t many people left in the classroom; most had gone to the canteen and the rest were asleep on their desks. The sunlight outside was lovely. It was November now, the sun no longer scorching; it fell on you warm and gentle, like a thin quilt.

Someone knocked on her desk.

She looked up.

Su Tang was standing by her desk holding a white plastic bag. In the bag was a disposable food box, still giving off a little steam that fogged the inside of the bag.

“For you.” Su Tang put the bag on her desk. “Old Zhou made too much today. Tomato beef rice.”

Gu Xuerong looked at the bag.

“…I’m not hungry.”

“I know,” said Su Tang, sitting backwards on the empty chair in front of her, both arms resting on the back, chin on her arms. “Just eat a couple of mouthfuls. Whatever you can’t finish, I’ll throw away for you.”

Gu Xuerong didn’t move.

Su Tang didn’t move either. She just looked at her, eyes bright, with a little smile, like a cat sitting by its food bowl, waiting.

After a while Gu Xuerong reached out, opened the plastic bag, took out the box and lifted the lid.

A puff of steam rose, carrying the sourness of tomato and the savour of beef. Over the rice was a layer of glossy red tomato sauce, thin slices of beef soaking in it, their edges curled slightly from the cooking; beside them a few pieces of tomato cooked soft, and half a soft-boiled egg, its yolk orange, pressing a little hollow into the rice.

She picked up the disposable chopsticks and snapped them apart, not quite evenly, one long and one short.

She picked up a slice of beef and put it in her mouth.

Su Tang watched from opposite, saying nothing, not smiling either, only shifting her chin on her arms to get a little more comfortable.

Outside the window, a few sparrows were chirping in the poplars by the sports field. From the direction of the canteen far off came the clatter of stainless-steel trays.

Gu Xuerong ate a mouthful of rice.

Then another.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

She ate a little less than half.

Su Tang packed the rest back in the plastic bag for her, tied it, carried it to the bin at the back of the classroom and threw it in.

“There’s more tomorrow,” said Su Tang. “Tomorrow it’s curry.”

“…No need.”

“Old Zhou says he makes too much every lunchtime,” said Su Tang. “He says his hand shakes, he can’t help it. If you don’t eat it, it’s wasted. Wasting food gets you struck by lightning.”

Gu Xuerong looked at her.

“Old Zhou’s hand doesn’t shake.”

“It does,” said Su Tang. “You just haven’t seen it.”

She stood up, pushed the chair back into place, brushed the dust off her trousers, waved to Gu Xuerong and went out of the front door, her footsteps bouncing away down the corridor.

Gu Xuerong sat at her desk looking at the front door.

After a while she turned and looked at the row behind her.

Ye Zhixing was lying on his desk, face buried in his arms, as if asleep.

She looked at him for a while.

Then she turned back, took the out-of-date bun out of her desk, stood up, walked to the back of the classroom and threw it in the bin. As it went in, the bun landed on top of the plastic bag with the food box in it, with a very soft sound.

She walked back to her seat and put her head down.

Under his arms, Ye Zhixing opened his eyes and looked at the back of her head for a while, then closed them again.

# Chapter Ten　Winter Clothes

## 1. Cold

The cold came early that year.

By the end of October the county town’s mornings had started to freeze. First a very thin skin of ice on the puddles by the road, thin as a sweet wrapper, that broke with a crack when you stepped on it; a few days later the ice was thicker and wouldn’t break, and the people setting out early for school slid with every step on it. Someone fell, the contents of their schoolbag spilled everywhere, and the wind chased their test papers into the middle of the road.

The two old camphor trees at the school gate were wilted by the frost too, the edges of their leaves curled, covered in a greyish-white rime. The popsicle tricycle had stopped coming long ago, replaced by an old man selling roast sweet potatoes, pushing a stove made out of an oil drum with a ring of sweet potatoes on top, roasted black outside and golden when you broke them open, steaming. The old man wore a fur-lined cap with earflaps tied in a knot under his chin, his face red with cold, and when he called out his wares, puffs of white breath came from his mouth.

In mid-November came the first snow.

It wasn’t heavy, just fine flakes that melted when they touched the ground and only settled in a thin layer on roofs and the tops of cars. Between classes the students crowded at the corridor windows to watch; someone put a hand out to catch one, caught a flake, and before they could see its shape it had turned into a drop of water.

Three days later came the second.

This one fell all night. In the morning, when you pushed the door open, the whole of Back Street was white, dazzlingly white. Snow had settled in a line along the copy shop’s shutter, and the owner was sweeping it down with a broom; each stroke brought a patch of snow pattering down at her feet. The thick plastic curtain at the internet café door had frozen stiff and creaked when you lifted it. The braised-meat stall had stopped coming altogether, and its patch of ground was buried in snow, impossible to tell what it had been. The second-floor windows were covered in frost flowers, growing in from the four corners of the glass towards the middle, feather after feather, as if someone had spent all night drawing on it in white pen.

The old people of the county town said they hadn’t seen snow like this in decades.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

No. 8 High’s rules didn’t change because of the snow.

School uniform was compulsory. Anyone not in uniform wasn’t allowed through the gate.

Two students on duty stood at the gate in red armbands, one on each side, like a pair of door gods. Every student coming through got a look from them. The uniform jacket had to be outermost; you could leave it unzipped, but those two blue-and-white stripes had to show. Someone who had put a down jacket over his uniform was stopped and told to take the down jacket off, uniform on the outside, down jacket on the inside.

“It won’t fit!”

“Then don’t wear the down jacket.”

“I’ll freeze to death!”

“Rules are rules.”

The student stood at the gate looking at the puffy down jacket in his hands and then at the thin uniform on his body, swore, stuffed the down jacket into his schoolbag and went in wearing the uniform, neck hunched, both hands pushed into his sleeves, like a plucked chicken.

The winter uniform had been handed out at the start of term but they had only been allowed to change into it at the end of October. A jacket and a pair of trousers, dark blue with white stripes, a thin layer of fleece inside: soft to touch, soft to wear, and no use against the wind. The wind poured in at the collar, in at the cuffs, in at the hem, went once round your body and slipped out somewhere else, leaving nothing behind but cold.

Most students’ parents had found a way. Under the uniform went thermal underwear, jumpers, fleece, vests, layer on layer, until the uniform jacket would hardly zip. One chubby boy wore three jumpers under his uniform, so that his arms wouldn’t hang down when he walked and he had to hold them out, like a penguin.

After that everyone knew: uniform on the outside, and what was underneath, nobody cared.

## 2. Treasures

Ye Zhixing and Chen Xi didn’t wear uniform.

Not secretly. Openly.

At the start of November the school’s competition coach found the two of them and asked whether they would enter the senior high division of the maths and physics olympiads. Province-wide: preliminary round next spring, then a semi-final for those who passed, then a final, and a place in the final meant guaranteed university admission, bonus points, the lot.
