No. 8 High hadn’t produced a provincial first prize in years, and the principal had said several times at staff meetings that this was the school’s “weak spot.”

The coach was a physics teacher in his fifties called Wu, very tall, a little stooped, thin on top, always in a blue Mao jacket washed pale. He brought the two of them to an empty lab, which smelled of formalin and rust mixed together, put a test paper in front of each of them and said: do it, no time limit, do as much as you can.

Ye Zhixing worked for two hours and handed it in.

Chen Xi worked for an hour and a half and handed it in.

Mr. Wu sat behind the lab bench with the two papers and read them. He took off his glasses, wiped them, put them back on and read them again. Then he put the papers down and looked at the two students in front of him, one in a grey hoodie, one in a black skull T-shirt with an army-green padded jacket over it, until both of them started to feel uneasy.

“…You two,” he said. “From tomorrow, you don’t need to go to morning lessons. Come here.”

And so that was how things went.

Ye Zhixing and Chen Xi came to the lab at nine every morning and left at five in the afternoon, sorting out their own lunch and midday rest. They didn’t have to attend morning reading, regular lessons or evening study, didn’t have to go to the flag-raising ceremony, didn’t have to wear uniform. The duty students at the gate just nodded when they saw them, barely even looking.

Once a new duty student who didn’t know them put out a hand to stop Chen Xi. “Hey, where’s your uniform?”

Chen Xi stopped, looked at him, and pointed to the lab window at the very top of the teaching block.

“I’m Mr. Wu’s.”

The duty student froze. The older one beside him tugged his sleeve and said something under his breath. The new one’s face went red at once, and he quickly drew his hand back.

“…Sorry.”

Chen Xi patted him on the shoulder and walked on.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

At school the two of them had become a pair of “treasures.”

Teachers spoke to them in a different tone. The canteen lady dug her ladle in a little deeper when she saw them. The head of year, meeting them in the corridor out of uniform, not only said nothing but would stop to ask, “Cold? Is the heating in the lab enough?”

The lab had no heating. Mr. Wu had paid for an electric heater out of his own pocket and put it between the two of them, with two pairs of gloves and a hot-water bottle warming on top of it.

Ye Zhixing wore a dark grey down coat, very thick, very long, down to his knees, with a ring of black fur round the collar; when he sat at the lab bench doing problems, its hem trailed on the floor. Chen Xi wore that army-green padded jacket, which his dad used to wear on building sites. The cuffs had worn through to show the stuffing, and he had wrapped them twice round with black electrical tape, very neatly.

When the two of them worked, they didn’t talk.

By the end of a morning, two stacks of scrap paper had piled up on the lab bench. Ye Zhixing’s was neat, line after line, as if printed; Chen Xi’s was a mess, the writing slanting, some places covered in diagrams with arrows pointing everywhere, some places half a line written and crossed out and started again alongside.

Mr. Wu came in at midday to have a look, leafed through the two stacks, said nothing, turned the heater up a notch, and went out.

## 3. Thin Clothes

Xuerong and the others weren’t so lucky.

Su Tang’s mum had knitted her a jumper, bright red, with a ring of white lace at the collar, the stitches very tight, knitted stitch by stitch in the evenings in front of the TV. Su Tang wore it under her uniform, and every day when she reached the shop, the first thing she did was take off her uniform jacket to show the red jumper, stand in front of the heater, turn round once and say, “I live again.”

Lin Xiaoman’s parents sent a parcel from Guangdong: two sets of thermal underwear, one pink and one grey, a pair of woollen gloves, a scarf, and a letter. The letter was very short, only a few lines, written by her mum in wobbly characters, and the last line was “It’s getting cold, wrap up warm, don’t catch a chill.” Lin Xiaoman read the letter three times, folded it and put it under her pillow, then put on the pink thermals and did a twirl round the room, saying, “It’s like wearing a quilt.”

The grey set she put on Gu Xuerong’s bed.

“My mum sent too many,” she said. “I can’t wear two sets.”

Gu Xuerong looked at the neatly folded grey thermals on the bed for a long time.

“…Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.” Lin Xiaoman climbed back up to her bunk. “Try them on, see if they fit.”

They didn’t really fit.

Lin Xiaoman was a size bigger than Gu Xuerong. On Gu Xuerong the thermals left a gap at the shoulders, the sleeves were too long, and the waistband had to be folded over twice to stay up. Gu Xuerong wore them under her uniform, sleeves rolled up twice to the wrist, with the uniform sleeves pulled down over them.

She was still cold.

It wasn’t that the clothes weren’t thick enough. It was that there was nothing on her.

She was too thin. So thin that bone lay right against skin and skin right against clothes, with nothing in between: no flesh, no fat, no layer to hold the warmth in. The wind poured in at the collar of her uniform, through the grey thermals and straight onto her bones, like hitting an iron railing, ting, cold all the way through.

On the fifteen-minute walk from the dormitory to school in the morning, her fingers went numb. The fingertips went white, then purple, then no colour at all, as if made of wax. She pushed her hands into her uniform pockets, but the pockets were thin; hands in or out made little difference.

In lessons she clamped both hands between her knees, clamped them tight, and her fingertips were still cold.

Her lips were always bluish.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

One morning the snow was especially heavy.

When Gu Xuerong reached the school gate there was snow in her hair, on her shoulders, on her eyelashes. She walked very slowly, step by step, leaving very shallow footprints in the snow—she was too light to sink in deep. The duty student looked at her, saw the uniform, nodded and let her in.

She went into the teaching block, up to the fourth floor, into Class Seven’s classroom, to her own seat, and sat down.

Her hands were shaking. Not the fine kind of tremble: the whole hand shaking, so much her fingers couldn’t meet. She tried to unzip her schoolbag; three times she tried, and three times the zip pull slid out from between her fingers.

A hand reached over from behind.

In it was something square, flat and soft, printed with a little bear.

A heat pack.

Gu Xuerong turned round. It was Lin Xiaoman. At some point Lin Xiaoman had come over from her own seat and was crouched in the aisle holding the heat pack, already unwrapped, already rubbed warm.

“Stick it on your tummy,” Lin Xiaoman said quietly. “On your tummy’s warmest. I brought a whole box.”

Gu Xuerong looked at the heat pack.

She took it and stuck it on her stomach, over the grey thermals.

At first she felt nothing. After a minute, two minutes, there was a little warmth, spreading slowly outward from her stomach, to her waist, to her chest, to her back. Very slowly, like the winter sun coming out from behind a cloud: at first just a little brighter, and only then, gradually, warm.

Her hands were still shaking, but not so badly.

Lin Xiaoman had already gone back to her own seat and was lying on her desk, pretending to read.

## 4. Chen Xi’s Lessons

One day at the end of October, Gu Xuerong got a friend request.

It was from Chen Xi. The verification message said:

> brother ye told me to add you says youre not great at maths ill teach you  

She looked at the message, her finger hovering over “Accept” for ages before she pressed it.

A photo came through at once: a sheet of scrap paper with a wonky little stick figure on it, holding up a sign that said “Hi.”

Then another message:

> what dont you get where do we start  

Gu Xuerong thought, and replied:

> all of it  

The other end went quiet for a while.

> all of it as in how much  

> i dont get middle school stuff either  

Another pause.

Then Chen Xi sent a voice message, thirty seconds. She held the phone to her ear to listen.

“Okay.” Chen Xi’s voice was a bit hoarse, with keyboards clattering in the background and Abiao yelling “Go, Brother Xi!” “Then we start with middle school. Don’t worry, there isn’t much to middle school, it’s three years of stuff, and if you really work at it you can catch up in two months. I’m telling you, all that middle school stuff is really just a few ideas, explained over and over. Get those few ideas straight and every problem after that looks the same.”

At the end his voice stopped for a moment, and then he added:

“…And the way I teach isn’t how the teachers teach. Teachers teach you how to do the problems. I teach you what the thing actually is.”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Chen Xi really did teach differently.

He didn’t explain formulas. He explained things.

For levers, he sent photos: on his desk, a chopstick balanced on an eraser, one coin on one end of the chopstick, three coins on the other. He pushed the eraser towards the three coins, a little at a time, taking a photo each time, until the chopstick was level.

> see the pivots close to the heavy side and far from the light side and it balances  
> force times distance same on both sides  
> thats all it is  
> the textbook takes two pages but its really just that one line  

For buoyancy, he sent a video. A red plastic basin full of water, three little fish swimming in it, crucian carp, dull grey, idling their tails along the bottom. He pushed an empty plastic bottle under the water and let go, and the bottle shot back up. Then he filled the bottle with water, pushed it under and let go, and the bottle slowly sank, down to the bottom of the basin, landing next to a fish, which got a fright and flicked away.

> the empty bottles got air in it lighter than the water it pushes aside so it floats up  
> fill it with water same weight as water so it sinks  
> fish can float or sink because theyve got a swim bladder inside like this bottle air in they go up air out they go down  
> caught these three at the river the day before yesterday do you want one ill give you one  

Gu Xuerong watched the video three times. It wasn’t the bottle she was watching. It was the three fish.

She replied:

> no theres cats at the shop  

> oh right the cats would eat it  

> yeah  

> ill keep them then if you want to see them ill film them for you  

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Little by little, she learned things about Chen Xi.

Not because he told her. They slipped out while he was explaining problems.

He said he had grown up in a village with no toys, so he made his own. With scrap wire and dead batteries his dad picked up on building sites, a little bulb, and a drink can cut open and flattened for a reflector, he made a torch and went out into the fields at night to look for frogs. He made a little car using the motor from a broken toy racer, a plank for the body and four mineral-water bottle caps for wheels, and the first time he drove it, it went straight into the pigsty. He made other things nobody else could make sense of: a windmill that turned by itself, a little pump that could lift water from low ground to high, and a trap for catching field mice, which worked so well that it caught one of his grandma’s chickens too, and his grandma chased him halfway round the village with a broom.

He caught fish and kept them, crucian carp, loaches, eels and a little spotted fish he couldn’t name, in a washing-up tub with half its side broken. He kept frogs too, from tadpoles, watching them grow back legs, then front legs, their tails shrinking back little by little until they were frogs, and then they hopped out of the tub into the fields and never came back.

“I just wanted to know how they changed,” he said. “Where does the tail go? Eaten? Absorbed? I looked it up, and the book said apoptosis, cells killing themselves. So I looked up what apoptosis was, and looking that up I got to genes, and looking that up I got to chemistry, and looking that up I got to physics.”

He said that once he got to middle school, to make better toys he started reading science and engineering books. The books nobody borrowed from the county library, he borrowed one after another, for three years, until he had worked his way through every shelf in those few rows. Electrician’s handbooks, mechanical principles, chemistry experiments, introductory astronomy, and later some books he couldn’t really understand himself, university physics, quantum mechanics.

“I can’t really understand quantum mechanics either,” he said. “But some of the bits I did understand, they just felt so…”

He paused, as if looking for the word.

“…So unreasonable.”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

That night it was past one in the morning.

Gu Xuerong lay on the lower bunk in the dormitory, facing the wall, her phone held up in front of her. Lin Xiaoman was asleep on the top bunk, breathing evenly. The other two girls were asleep too, one grinding her teeth, one talking in her sleep.

Chen Xi sent a long block of text. Not about problems; not about anything. Just something he wanted to say.

> do you know why theres anything in the universe  
> i mean why theres us and the earth and the sun and the stars  
> by rights at the start of the universe there shouldve been nothing  
> at the big bang energy turned into matter but every time a particle of matter got made a particle of antimatter got made at the same time  
> normal and anti coming out in pairs  
> then when normal meets anti they annihilate and turn back into energy and nothing is left  
> so by rights the universe should be empty not a single particle left  
> but its not  
> theres a tiny bit more matter than antimatter  
> about one part in a billion more  
> a billion antimatter to a billion and one matter  
> the billion all annihilated and the one thats left over is us  
> all the stars all the people all the cats are that one  
> the universe was supposed to be symmetrical and it turned out not to be and that tiny bit of asymmetry became everything  
> why its not symmetrical nobody completely knows even now  
> i think thats so unreasonable  
> and so good  

Gu Xuerong looked at the text for a long time.

The light of the screen fell on the wall, on the water stain shaped like a rabbit.

She typed a few words:

> one in a billion  

And deleted them.

She typed something else:

> is this on the test  

The reply took a while:

> no hahaha  
> go to sleep tomorrow its quadratic functions  

She locked the phone and put it by her pillow.

She didn’t sleep. She lay with her eyes open, looking at the water stain on the wall; in the dark she couldn’t make it out, only a vague outline.

One in a billion.

She said the number once to herself.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

She started catching up.

From the first year of middle school. Positive and negative numbers, rational numbers, linear equations in one unknown, triangles, congruence, similarity, Pythagoras. Chapter after chapter, turning the pages very slowly.

She could only study at night. In the daytime she still slept through lessons; she couldn’t take in what the teachers said. Those worked examples, notes on the board, explanations, one after another, were like a train that wouldn’t stop, roaring past in front of her while she stood on the platform unable even to see where the doors were. Night was different. At nine she got back from the shop, ate Lin Xiaoman’s food, played a round of the game, and once Lin Xiaoman was asleep she turned the desk lamp down to its dimmest and took out the photos and voice messages Chen Xi had sent, looked at them one by one, listened to them one by one, then wrote in her scrap pad, photographed what she had written and sent it to Chen Xi. And Chen Xi—who didn’t seem to sleep much either—would reply even at two in the morning, telling her which parts were right and which were wrong, and why the wrong parts were wrong.

At first it was very slow. One night was enough to understand just one idea, and sometimes not even one.

Later it got a bit faster.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Every lunchtime, Su Tang brought the food.

Monday tomato beef, Tuesday curry, Wednesday Yangzhou fried rice, Thursday omelette rice, Friday sizzling pickled cabbage and beef. Every day Old Zhou had “made too much,” his “hand shook,” he “couldn’t help it.” At ten past twelve on the dot every day Su Tang appeared at Class Seven’s door with a white plastic bag, sat backwards on the empty chair in front of Gu Xuerong, chin on the chair back, and watched her eat.

At first she ate a little less than half.

Later, half.

Later still, one day, Su Tang looked down into the box and found it empty. Every grain of rice was gone, just a little tomato juice left, drawing a red arc round the bottom of the box.

Su Tang stared at the empty box for several seconds.

She said nothing. She put the lid on, put the box in the plastic bag, tied it, and took it to the bin. On her way back from the bin she was bouncing as she walked, and halfway back she turned round and gave a thumbs-up to Ye Zhixing, lying on his desk in the row behind Xuerong.

Ye Zhixing lay there with his eyes closed, as if he hadn’t seen.

But the corner of his mouth moved.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

At the end of November, Gu Xuerong weighed herself.

Lin Xiaoman dragged her along. Outside the little shop at the foot of the dormitory block stood an old set of scales: put in a one-yuan coin and it read out the number in a shrill electronic voice. Lin Xiaoman went first, it read out a number, and she wailed that she had put on weight again; then she pushed Gu Xuerong on.

The scales read out a number.

Lin Xiaoman tilted her head and worked it out, and her eyes lit up.

“Three jin more!” she said. “Xuerong, you’ve put on three jin!”

Gu Xuerong stood on the scales looking down at the number.

Three jin. A kilo and a half.

She had no real sense of how much that was. She only knew that lately, when she got up in the morning, her head didn’t spin so much. On the stairs she didn’t have to stop at the third floor and hold on to the wall. When her fingers went white with cold, they didn’t turn purple so fast.

And lately, when she did a test paper, she could get through it.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

It was a short maths quiz. Twenty multiple-choice questions and four long ones.

Ms. Li handed out the papers. Gu Xuerong looked at the first question for a while, picked up her pen, and wrote down the answer.

The second question, she could do too.

The third, the fourth, the fifth.

Partway through, she suddenly stopped, looked up at the blackboard, at the old formulas layered over each other that would never wipe clean, and looked at them for a while, as if noticing for the first time that they had been there all along.

She pulled out the lever drawing Chen Xi had done for her from her workbook and laid it next to the paper. A look at the drawing, a look at the problem, another look at the drawing. Her pen tip tapped the scrap paper twice, then came down.

She looked down and carried on.

She got sixty-eight on that paper.

Not high. Class Seven’s average was a hundred and two.

But on the last quiz, she had got twenty-one.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

When Ms. Li was handing back the papers at the lectern, she reached Gu Xuerong’s name and paused.

She looked down at the score on the paper, then up at Gu Xuerong, and pushed up her glasses; the glasses chain swung.

“Gu Xuerong,” she said, “a big improvement.”

The whole class turned to look.

Gu Xuerong stood up to collect her paper. She went to the front, and Ms. Li handed her the paper, and as she did, her finger tapped the “68” on it, very lightly.

“Keep going,” said Ms. Li.

Gu Xuerong took the paper and went back to her seat.

She folded the paper up and put it in the innermost pocket of her schoolbag.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Then the physics teacher said it too. And the chemistry teacher. The English teacher said in class, “Some of you have improved very noticeably lately,” and as she said it her eyes flicked to the second row by the window.

Only the homeroom teacher, Zheng Xin, said nothing.

In the office, Zheng Xin spread out Gu Xuerong’s last few score sheets and laid them in order by date.

Twenty-one, thirty-five, forty-two, sixty-eight.

She stacked the score sheets together and put them in a folder.

Zheng Xin had moved over from Year Two. When she took over Class Seven, Mr. Sun had left behind a sheaf of “students requiring close attention,” and the first name on the list was Gu Xuerong, followed by a few lines: “Does not obey rules,” “Does not take part in collective duties,” “Parent uncooperative,” “Recommend she be advised to leave.” She read those lines, tore the page out, crumpled it into a ball and threw it in the wastepaper basket.

She never once made Gu Xuerong do the cleaning.

Nor did she do anything about Gu Xuerong sleeping in lessons. When Gu Xuerong was lying on her desk, Zheng Xin would walk round as she taught, and when she reached the window row, her steps would get a little lighter.

A teacher in the office once asked her: Ms. Zheng, that Gu Xuerong in your class sleeps in lessons every day, aren’t you going to do something about it?

Zheng Xin said: her scores are going up.

The teacher said: but she sleeps every day.

Zheng Xin said: ten lessons a day and four more in the evening, fourteen lessons, everyone sleeps sometimes. The school made the timetable, not me, and not her. If she can bring her scores up, those are our class’s scores. Not breaking her is the best thing we can do.

The teacher looked at her for a while and said nothing more.

## 5. Auntie

The good days didn’t last long.

It was a Thursday lunchtime, twenty past twelve.

The snow had stopped and the sun was out, shining on the thick snow covering the sports field, dazzlingly white. The classroom was quiet; most people had gone to the canteen and the rest were asleep on their desks. The radiators had only been lit the week before and weren’t very hot, just lukewarm to the touch; a few girls had their hands pressed flat against them and weren’t moving.

Gu Xuerong was eating.

Su Tang sat on the empty chair in front of her, chin on the chair back, watching her eat. It was Thursday, omelette rice, the egg fried golden, with a wonky cat drawn on top in ketchup. Su Tang had drawn it at the shop, and it looked like a pig.

Ye Zhixing and Chen Xi were there too.

They had just come back from the lab to fetch something. Ye Zhixing stood by his seat going through his schoolbag; Chen Xi leaned against the frame of the back door holding a roast sweet potato from the old man at the gate, peeling and eating it as he went, hissing at the heat.

The classroom’s front door was pushed open.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

A woman stood in the doorway.

She was about forty, with a tight perm of small curls dyed a reddish brown, an inch of black grown out at the roots. She wore a long rose-pink down coat, very new, as if the tag had only just been cut off, with a fluffy fake-fur collar that still had a bit of snow on it. Her face was powdered very white, so white it was a different colour from her neck. Her lips were painted very red. Gold hoop earrings hung from her ears, very big, swinging whenever she moved.

Both her hands were full. In her left was a big plastic bag of fruit, apples, oranges and bananas, bulging; in her right an even bigger woven bag, the red, white and blue striped kind, its mouth tied with string, stuffed full of something you couldn’t make out.

She stood in the doorway and swept her eyes round the classroom.

They reached the second row by the window and stopped.

“Rongrong!”

Her voice shot up all at once, high as if she were singing.

“Oh, Rongrong, I’ve finally found you!”

Carrying the two bags, in a pair of black ankle boots, she clicked into the room, past row after row of desks, to Gu Xuerong’s side, and dumped both bags in the aisle. As they landed, the fruit rolled inside, and an orange tumbled out of the bag and rolled to Su Tang’s feet.

Gu Xuerong held her spoon and didn’t move.

The spoon stopped in mid-air, just above the ketchup cat on the omelette rice.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

“Hello, everyone, hello.” The woman turned and smiled at the few students who had lifted their heads, smiling until her eyes were two slits and the powder at their corners creased into fine lines. “I’m Xuerong’s mum—”

She paused, very briefly, almost imperceptibly.

“—her auntie. Her dad asked me to come and see her.”

She bent down, took a handful of oranges out of the fruit bag and set one on each of the nearby students’ desks. “Here, here, have an orange, have an orange. Our Rongrong, she’s been sickly since she was little, and she’s got an odd temper, doesn’t talk much, I’m sure she’s caused you all plenty of trouble at school. Bear with her, won’t you, look after her a bit.”

She went over to Su Tang, bent down, pressed an orange into Su Tang’s hand, and pinched Su Tang’s cheek while she was at it.

“Oh my, what a pretty girl. You must be Rongrong’s best friend?”

Su Tang held the orange blankly, not sure whether to nod or shake her head.

“…I’m from the class next door.”

“Next door’s a good friend too,” said the woman. “With friends like you, Auntie can rest easy.”

She turned and saw Ye Zhixing, and her eyes stopped on him, swept over him from head to foot, over his long dark-grey down coat, over the ring of black fur round its collar, down to the shoes on his feet, and paused there.

Her smile deepened a little at once.

“And this young man must be Rongrong’s classmate too?” She took the biggest apple out of the bag, a shiny red, and held it out with both hands. “Here, Auntie’s treat, have an apple.”

Ye Zhixing looked at the apple.

“Thank you, Auntie,” he said. “I don’t eat apples.”

The woman’s hand stopped in mid-air. Only for a moment; she quickly drew it back, put the apple back in the bag, and said with a smile, “Oh, not eating apples is good, not eating apples is good, apples are all waxed these days, it’s not healthy.”

Last of all she noticed Chen Xi at the door.

Chen Xi was still leaning on the door frame holding the half-eaten sweet potato, steam rising from it. He looked at her, still chewing, and said nothing.

The woman’s eyes rested on Chen Xi’s face for a while. On the faint scar, almost healed, at the corner of his mouth.

Her smile didn’t change, but her eyes changed a little.

A very little, like a pebble dropped into a very deep well: only a faint ring on the surface, quickly smoothed away.

“And this young man,” she said, “is Rongrong’s classmate too?”

“Yeah,” said Chen Xi.

“What’s your name, then?”

Chen Xi took another bite of sweet potato, chewed it slowly, and swallowed.

“Auntie,” he said, “you dropped an orange.”

The woman looked down: the orange by Su Tang’s feet was still on the floor. She bent to pick it up with a smile, wiped it on her down coat and stuffed it back in the bag. When she looked up again, Chen Xi had already turned and gone out, dropping the sweet-potato skin into the bin by the door.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

She went back to Gu Xuerong’s seat.

“Rongrong,” she said, lifting the woven bag onto Gu Xuerong’s desk, where it pressed down on one corner of the omelette rice, “it’s getting cold, and your dad was worried you’d freeze, so he had me bring you a few winter things. Have a look, see if they fit.”

She untied the string at the mouth of the bag and pulled out a down jacket.

Pink, short, with a yellow stain on one cuff that wouldn’t wash out, the zip pull on the collar missing and replaced with a paper clip. The jacket was very narrow in the shoulders and very short in the hem: made for a child shorter and smaller than Gu Xuerong.

Behind it came two jumpers, a pair of padded trousers and a pair of woollen socks. The jumpers were badly bobbled, lumpy to the touch. The padded trousers had a patch on one knee, the patch a different colour from the trousers.

“They’re all good clothes, all good clothes,” said the woman, shaking them out one by one and holding each one up against Gu Xuerong. “Your little sister’s grown out of them, they’re still as good as new, they’ll fit you perfectly. Look at this down jacket, isn’t it pretty, pink, girls look best in pink.”

Gu Xuerong sat there and let her hold them up.

She didn’t move and didn’t speak, just sat there, spoon still in her hand, watching the woman’s hands shake out the clothes in front of her one by one.

When she had finished, the woman folded the clothes, stuffed them back in the woven bag, and took a small red envelope out of her coat pocket, the character for “Fortune” printed on it in gold.

“And this.” She pushed the envelope into Gu Xuerong’s hand, pushing hard, her voice rising again, high enough for the whole classroom to hear. “Two hundred yuan, living money from your dad. Your dad says it’s not easy for you out here on your own, you should eat better, dress warmer, don’t be stingy with yourself. If it’s not enough, tell the family.”

Gu Xuerong looked down at the red envelope in her hand.

The woman bent down, close to her ear, and her voice dropped all at once, so low that only Gu Xuerong could hear it, low like a snake sliding through the grass.

“…Your dad says, come home for New Year.”

She straightened up and smiled again, smiling her eyes into two slits.

“Well, Auntie’s off then. Rongrong, study hard, listen to your teachers, get on with your classmates.” She waved to the students in the room. “Bye, everyone, look after our Rongrong for us.”

She picked up the half-empty fruit bag and clicked out in her black ankle boots.

At the door, she looked back.

Not at Gu Xuerong. At the woven bag, the woven bag on Gu Xuerong’s desk, as if checking it was still there.

Then she was gone. Her footsteps sounded in the corridor for a while, further and further, down the stairs, and couldn’t be heard any more.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

The classroom was very quiet.

The few students who had been given oranges looked at each other. Someone said quietly, “Her auntie’s nice,” someone said, “The oranges are sweet,” and peeled them and ate them.

Su Tang looked down at the orange in her hand.

Gu Xuerong put the red envelope down on her desk. Next to the woven bag, next to the omelette rice.

She didn’t open it.

She picked up her spoon and went on eating.

The omelette rice had gone a bit cold. One ear of the ketchup cat on top had been squashed flat by the woven bag, the ketchup smeared into a blob, so that it looked even more like a pig.

She ate spoonful by spoonful, very slowly, very carefully, eating every last grain of rice.

When she had finished, she put the lid on the box, put it in the plastic bag, tied it and handed it to Su Tang.

“Thank you.”

Su Tang took it and looked at her; her mouth opened, and nothing came out.

She lifted the woven bag off the desk, retied the string at its mouth, tied it twice, pushed it under the desk and nudged it further in with her foot, until it couldn’t be seen. She brought the bag of fruit over too and put it next to the woven bag.

The red envelope she put in her uniform pocket.

From the moment that woman came in to the moment she left, she hadn’t said a single word to her.

Then she put her head down.

Forehead against her arm, her right hand gripping her left cuff.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}

Ye Zhixing stood by his seat, his schoolbag zip halfway closed, and never finished closing it.

He was looking under her desk. One corner of the red, white and blue woven bag stuck out, bulging, its string neatly tied.

He thought of that pink down jacket. Short, narrow-shouldered, a yellow stain on the cuff, the zip pull replaced with a paper clip.

“Your little sister’s grown out of them.”

He thought of the way that woman had looked at him. Head to foot, stopping at his coat, stopping at his shoes.

He thought of the way she had looked at Chen Xi. Stopping at the scar at the corner of Chen Xi’s mouth.

He thought of that last look back. At the woven bag, not at the person.

He thought of what she had said, bending down to Gu Xuerong’s ear. He hadn’t heard what it was. He had only seen Gu Xuerong’s hand, the one holding the spoon, its knuckles go white for an instant.

He zipped his bag shut.

Chen Xi was in the corridor.

He stood by a window that was open a crack, cold wind pouring through and stirring the hair on his forehead. He was still holding the sweet-potato wrapping paper, crushed into a ball.

Ye Zhixing came out of the classroom and stopped beside him.

Neither of them spoke.

Outside, the snow on the sports field was dazzlingly white. A figure in a rose-pink down coat was coming out from the bottom of the teaching block, walking along the path swept clear at the edge of the field, towards the school gate. She walked fast, the hem of her coat swinging. At the gate she stopped, took out her phone and made a call.

It was too far to hear what she was saying. They could only see her holding the phone in one hand and gesturing with the other, gesturing for quite a while.

Then she hung up, walked out of the gate, and was gone.

“She asked my name,” said Chen Xi.

“Yeah, I heard.”

“She saw this thing on my lip.”

“She looks at everyone like she’s weighing them.”

Chen Xi squeezed the ball of paper in his hand a little tighter.

“That jacket,” he said, “wasn’t her little sister’s.”

Ye Zhixing said nothing.

“She said her little sister had grown out of it,” said Chen Xi. “That down jacket, I saw the label at the collar. It’s a kids’ brand, size 120. A hundred and twenty, that’s for a seven- or eight-year-old. If Gu Xuerong’s little sister is seven or eight, then she’s that woman’s kid with her dad.”

He paused.

“…Clothes a seven- or eight-year-old has grown out of, given to a sixteen-year-old.”

Ye Zhixing still said nothing.

He was looking at the swept path outside, at the place where that person had just walked: a line of footprints left in the snow, the holes made by her heels one after another, very deep.

“Two hundred yuan,” said Chen Xi. “Handed over in front of the whole class.”

“Yeah.”

“She was worried people wouldn’t know.”

Ye Zhixing turned to look at him.

Chen Xi was looking at him too. Chen Xi’s eyes were very bright, frighteningly bright, the same brightness as when he was staring at a problem in the lab that he couldn’t crack.

They looked at each other for a while.

Neither of them said the thing out loud.

“…Let’s get back to the lab,” said Ye Zhixing. “Mr. Wu’s doing electromagnetic induction this afternoon.”

“Yeah.”

They went downstairs, one behind the other.

At the turn on the third floor, Chen Xi stopped and looked back up. The fourth-floor corridor was empty; Class Seven’s door stood open a crack, and through the crack you could see only the window row, and a very thin back, lying on a desk.

He looked for a while, then turned back and went on down.

“Brother Ye.”

“Yeah.”

“That down jacket,” said Chen Xi. “Will she wear it?”

Ye Zhixing stopped.

He stood on the stairs and thought of how she had come into the classroom that morning, snow in her hair and on her eyelashes, hands shaking too much to open her schoolbag zip. Thought how, apart from this uniform, he couldn’t remember ever seeing her in anything else warm.

“…Probably,” he said.

“Size 120.”

Ye Zhixing didn’t answer.

Chen Xi glanced at him and didn’t go on either.

The two of them carried on down. The stairwell windows were covered in frost flowers, and the sun shining on them made a scatter of very bright broken light that fell on the steps and on their shoes, step after step, all the way down.

# Chapter Eleven　The Sand Table

## 1. Midnight

Lately Ye Zhixing had often been waking in the middle of the night.

Not from a nightmare, and not because some noise woke him. He was simply awake: his eyes opened, and he was as clear-headed as in daytime, and there was no getting back to sleep. He glanced at his phone, a little after two, or just past three, the light of the screen stinging his eyes, then turned the phone face down on the bedside table, lay there and looked at the ceiling.

There was nothing on the ceiling. White, flat, with the heat from the radiator floating against it, invisible, but he could feel it, a layer of dry, faintly hot air pressing on his face.

After lying there a while he would get up, walk barefoot to the planted aquarium and sit down on the floor in front of it.

The tank lights had long since gone off, leaving only the blue night light in one corner. In the dark the plants were black, clump after clump, like a shrunken forest. The neon tetras were asleep, hanging motionless in the gaps between the plants, the fluorescent blue line along their sides still faintly glowing in the dark, like a row of tiny indicator lights someone had forgotten to switch off. The CO₂ bubble counter had stopped too, on its timer. The whole tank was as still as a photograph.

He just sat there and watched.

Watched what, he couldn’t really have said himself. The piece of dragon stone, the small patch of moss growing at its foot, a fish that gave its tail one small flick in its sleep and then was still again.

He had built this tank in his second year of middle school. It was the first winter after everything was over, he couldn’t sleep night after night, so he went online and looked up how to keep fish, how to grow aquatic plants, how to adjust the water’s hardness, its pH, the concentration of CO₂. It took him three weeks to build it, and half a year more before it was stable. A batch of plants died, a batch of fish died, the algae bloomed twice, green as a tank of pea soup. He adjusted it bit by bit, looked for the cause bit by bit, and in the end it came alive.

Once it was alive, it stayed like this. Two years now: every day he changed a little of its water, trimmed a little of its plants, fed it a little, and it just went on living like this, no more, no less.

He liked it because it was a closed thing. All the numbers added up. How much light, how much CO₂, how much the fish excreted, how much the plants absorbed, what came in and what went out, in the end it balanced. If even one number was off, something would go wrong; and as long as you were willing to look, you could find which number was off.

The world outside wasn’t like that.

In the world outside, a lot of numbers didn’t add up. And some of the numbers that didn’t, you could see perfectly well, and there was still nothing you could do to touch them.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

He had started saying strange things in the daytime, too.

Once at the shop, Chen Xi was explaining a physics problem to Gu Xuerong, and got to conservation of energy. Ye Zhixing was behind the counter going over the accounts, and without looking up, he cut in:

“Money isn’t conserved.”

Chen Xi stopped for a second. “…What?”

“Energy is conserved, money isn’t,” said Ye Zhixing. “Money can be made out of nothing, and it can vanish into nothing. A bank lends you a million, and that million didn’t exist before; it only appears the second you sign. If one day you can’t pay it back, it’s gone again in a second. But that million that’s gone, somebody has already used it to put up buildings, buy cement, pay wages, and those things are real.”

He turned a page of the ledger.

“So when the money disappears, what disappears isn’t the money. It’s the things the people who got the money thought they owned.”

Chen Xi looked at him for a good while, then turned his head and said to Gu Xuerong, “…He didn’t sleep well today.”

Gu Xuerong looked at Ye Zhixing.

“He hasn’t slept well for days,” she said.

Ye Zhixing looked up at her. She had already turned back to her problem, her pencil drawing a block on the scrap paper, and under the block an inclined plane, drawn very carefully.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Another time, Su Tang was brushing the Ragdoll, and partway through she sighed and said her mum wanted her to apply to a teachers’ college later, teachers’ college was good, stable, after graduating she could come back to the county and be a teacher and never have to worry for the rest of her life.

“Do you want to be a teacher?” Ye Zhixing asked.

“Don’t know,” said Su Tang. “Never thought about it. If my mum says it’s good, then it’s good, I guess.”

Ye Zhixing didn’t answer. After a while, he said:

“This thing called stability, it’s only stable because nobody moves.”

Su Tang stopped the brush and looked up at him.

“A table with four legs, whether it’s steady or not doesn’t depend on whether the legs are strong, it depends on whether the ground is level,” he said. “If the ground tilts, it doesn’t matter how strong the legs are.”

“…What do you mean?”

Ye Zhixing opened his mouth, as if he wanted to explain, and in the end shook his head.

“Nothing,” he said. “Keep brushing. Your Highness is about to start swearing again.”

Sure enough, the Ragdoll let out a curse. Su Tang lowered her head and went on brushing, brushed a few strokes, then looked up again and glanced at him.

That glance stayed a little long.

## 2. The Recommendation

The Ye family had made their start in building materials.

More than twenty years ago, Ye Shilong opened a shopfront by the highway on the north side of the county town, selling cement, selling rebar, selling tiles, with a second-hand Dongfeng truck parked out front that he drove himself to make deliveries. Back then the tallest buildings in the county town were only six storeys, and his cement went up them one sack on someone’s shoulder at a time, until it had carried up the county town’s first eight-storey building, its first housing estate with lifts, its first pedestrian street.

Later he no longer just sold materials. He started acquiring land himself and putting up buildings himself.

These past few years had been the best years. The year before last the county had been upgraded to a city, land prices doubled every year, and the flats in a building sold out before it was even topped off. The Ye family had a development each in the east and the south of town, and had acquired another plot in the west, where piles were being driven now. The family’s building-materials company had grown from one shopfront into a whole street of warehouses, from one Dongfeng truck into a fleet.

It was on a Sunday afternoon that Ye Zhixing put the thing on his father’s desk.

He had made it himself. A dozen-odd pages, printed out, held together with a black binder clip. In it were the county’s population figures for the past five years, the resident population smaller every year; the sale prices and sell-through times of the county town’s main developments, the sell-through times longer every year; the debts on the Ye family’s projects, from accounts he had wheedled and pestered out of Uncle He and worked through item by item; and a few pages he had clipped from the news, where the phrase “houses are for living in, not for speculation” had been circled three times in red pen.

The last page had only one sentence:

> Recommendation: Stop acquiring new land. Slow down the west-side project. Gradually reduce debt.  

Ye Shilong sat behind the desk and turned the pages one by one.

He was in his early fifties, his hair combed back very neatly, already grey at the temples. He wore a dark cashmere cardigan and an old-style gold watch on his wrist, the band a little loose, so that it slid back and forth on his wrist as he turned the pages. He turned them slowly, read every page, and where there were numbers he would pause, and tap the number with one finger.

Ye Zhixing stood on the other side of the desk and waited.

The study was large. Three walls were bookshelves, and most of the books on them came in sets, hardbacks with gilt spines that hardly anyone had ever opened. The other wall was a big window, and outside it was the osmanthus tree in the courtyard, its leaves all fallen, a layer of snow lying along its branches, and when the wind blew the snow off, it fell with a soft rustle.

Ye Shilong turned the last page, closed the stack, clipped it back together with the binder clip and set it at the corner of the desk.

“Not bad work,” he said.

“The data is right,” said Ye Shilong. “People are leaving, flats aren’t moving, debt is rising. Everything you’ve said here, I already know.”

“Then why—”

“Because the things you’ve calculated,” Ye Shilong raised his head and looked at his son, “aren’t what matters most in this county town.”

His voice wasn’t loud, and it wasn’t hurried, and when he spoke there was a slight smile at the corners of his mouth, but the smile stopped at his mouth and never reached his eyes.

“Take this thing of yours to the city, to the province, show it to the banks, to the people who do research, and they’ll all say your figures are right. But here,” he tapped the desktop once with a finger, “in this place, whether buildings go up or not, whether land gets taken or not, doesn’t depend on data. It depends on people.”

“Which people?”

Ye Shilong didn’t answer. He stood up, walked over to the coat stand, took down the black overcoat hanging there and draped it over his arm.

“Don’t go to school tomorrow afternoon,” he said. “Come with me to meet someone.”

## 3. The Sand Table

At three the next afternoon, Ye Zhixing followed his father into the city government building.

It was an old building, put up in the eighties, five storeys, its outer walls faced with cream-coloured tiles, a few of which had already fallen off, showing the grey cement underneath. At the entrance were two pillars, and on the pillars hung signs, black characters on white, where the word “County” had been painted out and the word “City” written in beside it, its colour a little newer than the rest.

The mayor’s office was on the fourth floor.

The mayor was in his early forties, not tall, but full of energy, his hair cut very short, his face carrying the kind of keyed-up sheen that only people who are chronically short of sleep have. He wore a white shirt with the sleeves rolled to the forearm and no tie, and when he saw Ye Shilong come in he strode over, took Ye Shilong’s hand in both of his and shook it hard a few times.

“Old Ye, Old Ye, you’re here, you’re here.” He turned to look at Ye Zhixing, and his eyes lit up. “So this is your boy— I’ve heard about him, I’ve heard about him, top of his year, competition student, right? Good, good. The young will surpass us.”

He shook Ye Zhixing’s hand too. His hand was hot, dry, his grip very strong.

There were several other people in the office.

All middle-aged men, sitting on a row of sofas against the wall, in much the same dark jackets, some fat, some thin, and when they saw Ye Shilong come in they all stood, smiling and greeting him as “Mr. Ye”. Ye Zhixing recognized two of them, the bosses of two other small developers in the county, one named Liu, one named Ma, who had come to the house at New Year to pay their respects, carrying Moutai.

They were all smiling. Smiling very happily, as if they had just heard some good news.

In the middle of the office stood a very big table, and on the table was a sand table model.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

The sand table was as big as a ping-pong table.

The whole county town was on it, shrunk thousands of times over, made out of plastic, foam and wood. The river on the east side, the two bridges over the river, the old street in the town centre, the schools, the hospital, the railway station, building after building, tree after tree, all made in fine detail. Ye Zhixing found No. 8 High on it, found Back Street behind No. 8 High, and on Back Street the little two-storey building, as small as a sugar cube.

On the north side of the sand table, a large area was empty.

Not actually empty: it was covered with a clear acrylic dome. The area under the dome was different from everywhere else on the sand table: the buildings were new, white, lined up block after block, perfectly neat, in a great square formation; in the middle of the formation was a plaza, and in the plaza a fountain; north of the plaza was a very tall, very wide building, with a tiny red flag stuck on its roof.

Ye Zhixing knew what that area used to be.

The north of town, the railway freight yard and the old grain depot. A few rows of red-brick warehouses, a disused railway line, a patch of self-built single-storey houses, several hundred households living in them, most of them old people. And the building-materials market, where Gu Jianguo carried cement, was right on the edge of it.

“This is our new district,” said the mayor, standing at the edge of the sand table, his hand resting on the acrylic dome. “The North City Area.”

His voice suddenly rose, as if he were in a meeting, or giving a speech.

“This city of ours has been upgraded from a county for two years now. But look,” his hand swept a circle over the sand table, “where’s our city centre? Still in the old town. And what’s the old town like? Narrow roads, old buildings, nowhere even to park. A city without a decent city centre, how is it supposed to attract business? Attract investment? Keep young people here?”

His hand moved to the area under the acrylic dome.

“So the city has decided: the North City Area will be completely redeveloped. The old warehouses, the old single-storey houses, all of it comes down. New housing estates, new schools, new hospitals, a new commercial centre.” He paused and looked around the room. “The land in this area, Mr. Ye, Mr. Liu, Mr. Ma, and a few others, it’s already been acquired.”

The men on the sofas smiled even wider.

Ye Zhixing looked at the sand table, at that stretch of white, neat new buildings. He thought of his own report, a dozen-odd pages, of those population figures, smaller every year.

He spoke up.

“Mayor,” he said, “how many people live in that northern area right now?”

The mayor turned to look at him, the glow of the speech still in his eyes. “About… eight hundred-odd households. There’s a plan for demolition compensation, everyone will be properly resettled.”

“And the new housing estates, how many households are planned?”

“Three thousand in phase one, another two thousand in phase two.”

“Five thousand households,” said Ye Zhixing. “The county town— the city has been losing more than ten thousand residents a year these past few years. Half the flats in the developments in the east and south still haven’t sold. Five thousand households. Who’s going to live there?”

The office went quiet for a moment.

Someone on the sofas gave a dry cough. Ye Shilong stood on the other side of the sand table and said nothing, watching his son, his expression very calm, as if he had known all along that he would ask this.

The mayor looked at Ye Zhixing for a while, then suddenly laughed.

The kind of laugh that was very generous, very indulgent, like an adult listening to a child talk.

“Good question, young Ye,” he said. “We’ve considered that question too. You’re right, if you just put up buildings and nobody comes to live in them, that won’t do.”

He reached out and pointed under the acrylic dome, at the tallest, widest building, the one with the little red flag.

“That’s why this, here,” he said, “is the new civic centre.”

Ye Zhixing’s gaze stopped on that building.

“The city government, the city Party committee, the People’s Congress, the Political Consultative Conference, and the court, the procuratorate, the public security bureau, the tax bureau, the education bureau, the health bureau,” the mayor counted them off one by one, his finger tapping one by one on the ring of small buildings around the big one, “all of them move over. The government leads the way, the public institutions lead the way, several thousand civil servants and public-sector employees, along with their families, all move to the North City. The schools follow, the hospitals follow, business follows.”

He drew his hand back and rested it on the acrylic dome, very steadily.

“That’s where the people come from.”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Ye Zhixing said nothing more.

He looked at the building with the little red flag.

This land wasn’t a development. It was a project that had to be built. The city government moving there was the biggest thing of the mayor’s term, something to be written into reports and shown to the people above. It couldn’t not be built, couldn’t be built slowly, couldn’t be built halfway and stopped.

So where would the money to build it come from?

From the people who had taken this land.

The demolition compensation, they would pay. The infrastructure, they would provide. The schools, the hospitals, the roads, the pipe networks, they would front the money. The new civic building, too, they might have to “build on the government’s behalf”, and once it was built, the government would “buy it back in instalments”— how many instalments, starting when, would be settled when the time came.

They would stake everything they had on it. And once it was staked, they could never pull it out again. Because once the buildings started going up, they couldn’t stop; if they stopped, everything put in before would be lost. They could only keep putting more in, until the day the buildings were finished, or until the day they couldn’t put in any more.

And the mayor, the mayor’s term had a number on it. Three years, five years. If the buildings were finished, he would be the man who “built the new district”, and he would move up. If they weren’t finished, he would still move up, or move somewhere else, and what would be left behind was a stretch of dug-up ground and a crowd of developers trapped inside it.

He took his eyes off the building and looked at the men on the sofas.

Mr. Liu was smiling. Mr. Ma was smiling. The other two, whose names he didn’t know, were smiling too, and one of them was saying something in a low voice to the man beside him, and when he got to the good part, slapped his thigh.

They were all far smaller developers than the Ye family. The Ye family had two developments, east and south; they had one each, and some of them hadn’t even sold out that one. In taking the land in the North City, they had staked their whole fortunes, their whole lives.

When the civic centre moved over, land prices would rise, house prices would rise, this land was gold.

Ye Zhixing looked at them, at the flushed, excited shine on their faces in the office the radiators had heated until it was scorching.

He opened his mouth.

In the end he said nothing.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

When they came out of the city government building, it was almost dark.

It had started snowing again, very fine, slanting through the light under the streetlamps. Uncle Chen brought the car round to the foot of the steps, Ye Shilong got in first, and Ye Zhixing stood on the steps and looked back once at the old cream-coloured building. The window on the fourth floor was still lit, and on it were the shadows of several people, moving back and forth.

He ducked into the car.

The car went a fair way, and Ye Shilong said nothing the whole time, looking out of the window.

After a long while, he spoke.

“You understand now.”

It wasn’t a question.

Ye Zhixing looked at the hands on his knees.

“…Why take it?” he asked. “You know perfectly well.”

Ye Shilong brought his gaze back from the window and looked at the wipers sweeping across the windscreen in front of them, back and forth.

“If I don’t take it,” he said, “the pre-sale permits for the two developments in the east and south won’t get approved next month.”

The wipers swept across, and swept back.

“You think that’s a piece of land,” said Ye Shilong. “It’s an admission ticket.”

## 4. The Banquet

The dinner was three evenings later, at the best hotel in the county town, in a private room on the top floor.

Ye Zhixing hadn’t wanted to go. His father said go, just sit there, you don’t have to say anything. So he went.

The room was large, with a big round table in the middle that could seat twenty. In the middle of the table was a motorized lazy Susan, already covered with cold dishes, ring after ring, arranged like a flower. On the wall hung a landscape painting of the Welcoming Pine on Mount Huang, with four characters inscribed beneath the pine: “Guests feel at home.” The light was a crystal chandelier, very bright, so bright that there was no shadow on anyone’s face.

A lot of people came.

All the developers from the North City came. Mr. Liu, Mr. Ma, and the two whose names he didn’t know. The director of the cement plant came, the boss of the steel company, the manager of the concrete mixing plant, the window-and-door people, the lift people, the waterproofing people. The president of a bank came and sat beside the seat of honour, in gold-rimmed glasses, saying little and smiling the whole time. A deputy director from the demolition office came, and a section chief from the housing and construction bureau.

Ye Shilong sat in the seat of honour.

Ye Zhixing sat on his father’s left, in the third seat, next to the director of the cement plant, a very fat middle-aged man with a thick gold chain round his neck.

The liquor was Moutai. A waitress carried in a case, opened it and set the bottles one by one on the lazy Susan.

Then the toasting began.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Ye Zhixing sat there and watched.

He watched his father stand, glass in hand, and toast them one by one, starting from the seat of honour. The bank president, the deputy director, the section chief, Mr. Liu and Mr. Ma, the director, the manager, the bosses. With each person, a few words, a clink of glasses, head back, glass drained. His father could hold his drink; seven or eight glasses in, his face wasn’t the least bit red, his voice hadn’t changed in the slightest, and that slight smile stayed at the corners of his mouth.

He watched the others stand one by one and toast his father back, toast other people, toast each other. The lazy Susan went round and round, and the dishes changed course after course. Lobster, abalone, sea cucumber, a steamed star-spotted grouper, its eyes white, bulging, staring at the ceiling.

He watched Mr. Liu get drunk, his face as red as a slab of pig’s liver, his arm round Mr. Ma’s shoulders, saying with a thick tongue, “Brother Ma, once the North City takes off, you and me, we go in together, take another plot, another plot…”

He watched the bank president, glass in hand, say something in a low voice to Ye Shilong, a sentence and then a smile, and Ye Shilong nodded and smiled too.

He watched the deputy director from the demolition office take out his phone, open a map, point at an area on it, and gesture to the section chief from the housing bureau. “This area, three months, within three months, all cleared. Work starts after Spring Festival.”

The section chief said, “There are a lot of old people in that area. Probably a fair few holdouts.”

The deputy director said, “There are ways.”

He watched the director of the cement plant, sitting beside him, pick up a big chopsticksful of sea cucumber and drop it into his bowl, then clap him on the shoulder and say, “Young Ye, your dad says your family’s building the new high school too. You’ll be studying in a school your own family built, how about that.”

Ye Zhixing looked down at the piece of sea cucumber in his bowl, black, soft, with a glistening layer of glaze on it.

“The new high school?”

“You didn’t know?” The director was surprised, and lowered his voice, his breath full of liquor in Ye Zhixing’s face. “Over in the North City, they’re building a new high school, a city key school, three times the size of No. 8 High. The government says your family builds it on their behalf. Once it’s built, No. 8 High’s senior section moves over there.”

“When will it be built?”

“Three years,” said the director, picking up a piece of abalone. “If all goes well, three years.”

He stuffed the abalone into his mouth, chewed twice, and added, indistinctly:

“…If it doesn’t go well, then it’s hard to say.”

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Ye Zhixing sat there right to the very end.

He didn’t drink a drop, and he hardly ate anything. He looked at the faces, one after another, flushed and shining, listened to the “bottoms up”, “Mr. Ye can really hold his drink”, “once the North City takes off we all get rich together”, watched the dishes taken away half eaten from the lazy Susan, watched the waitresses go in and out topping up the liquor, looked at the Welcoming Pine on the wall.

He felt something was wrong.

Not that the data was wrong. He had worked the data out long ago. It was another kind of wrong, one he couldn’t put into words, like a number in the aquarium that didn’t add up: you know perfectly well it’s there, and you just can’t find where.

He looked at his father.

Ye Shilong was clinking glasses with the bank president. Then head back, glass drained, glass set down, a dab at the corners of his mouth with his napkin, and he turned his head and met his son’s eyes.

Father and son, one seat apart, looked at each other for a second.

Ye Shilong’s eyes were clear. Not the least bit drunk, clear as glass just washed.

He gave his son a very small nod.

Then he turned back and went on talking to the others.

## 5. Downstairs

That weekend, at the cat café, Ye Zhixing told them about it.

He didn’t start with it. At first he said nothing at all, sitting on the grey sofa under the big screen with a controller in his hands, and on the screen was that rain-soaked corridor from Nightmare Raid, his character standing in the middle of the corridor, not moving.

Gu Xuerong sat beside him, holding a controller too. Her character stood beside his character, not moving either.

The two characters just stood like that, in that corridor where the rain kept falling, for nearly ten minutes.

Su Tang finished brushing the Ragdoll, came over, looked at the screen, then at the two of them.

“What are you doing?”

“Waiting,” said Gu Xuerong.

“Waiting for what?”

Gu Xuerong didn’t answer, and turned her head to look at Ye Zhixing.

Ye Zhixing put the controller down.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

He told it very slowly, in fits and starts. About his father, about the report, about the mayor, about the sand table, about the building with the red flag, about that dinner, about that piece of sea cucumber, about the North City that would be demolished in three months, about the new high school that wouldn’t be finished for three years.

He didn’t talk about the numbers, didn’t talk about debt, didn’t talk about sell-through times, didn’t say “an admission ticket”. He only told what he had seen and what he had heard.

Chen Xi had come too. He had come straight from the internet café, and halfway through he stopped playing on his phone and leaned against the arm of the sofa, listening.

Su Tang sat on the floor with her back against the sofa, hugging her knees.

Gu Xuerong kept looking at him the whole time.

When he finished, the room was very quiet. Calico yawned on the windowsill, and halfway through the yawn, seeing that nobody was moving, closed its mouth again. In the kitchen Old Zhou’s griddle sizzled, in bursts, sounding very far away.

“I don’t really understand,” Su Tang spoke first, very quietly. “Debt, civic centres… I don’t really understand.”

She hugged her knees, her chin resting on them, and thought for a moment.

“But where we live, across the river, the year before last they said it was getting demolished too,” she said. “They said they were building some kind of wetland park. They painted the red ‘demolish’ character on the walls, a circle with ‘demolish’ inside it, painted everywhere. There was one on our wall too. Back then my mum did sums every day, how much money we’d get if it was demolished, how many flats we could swap it for, said that way the money for me to go to university would be sorted.”

“It still hasn’t been demolished. That ‘demolish’ has faded, it’s turned pink. When it rains, the colour runs down the wall, in streaks. My mum doesn’t do the sums any more.”

She looked down at her trainers.

“…I just think, things people say they’ll do, they don’t necessarily do. And things they do, they don’t necessarily finish.”

Ye Zhixing looked at her.

Su Tang didn’t look up, picking with a finger at a bit of rubber on the side of her trainer, picked at it a while, then stopped.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Chen Xi scratched the back of his head.

“I don’t get this stuff either,” he said. “Property or whatever, nobody in my family has touched it in eight generations.”

He thought for a while.

“But I’ve only got one question,” he said. “Who’s buying?”

Ye Zhixing looked at him.

“Our village,” said Chen Xi, “when I was little, more than three hundred households. Now there’s fewer than a hundred left, and the ones left are all old people and kids. The young ones have all gone, Guangdong, Zhejiang, Shanghai. They come back for a few days at New Year, and after New Year they leave again. When they leave, some of them lock up their houses, lock them for a year, two years, lock them until the houses fall down and still don’t come back.”

He shoved his phone into his pocket.

“The county town’s the same. Forty-seven people in our class, go and ask, how many want to stay in the county town later? Not a single one. Everyone wants out. Out through university, out through work, out one way or another.”

He grinned, a slightly dry grin.

“Me too. I’m not staying here. I’m leaving, as far as I can get. Beijing, Shanghai, abroad, anywhere. As long as it’s not here.”

He looked at Ye Zhixing.

“So when you say they’re building five thousand homes,” he said, “all I want to ask is, who’s buying? And who lives in them once they’re bought?”

He didn’t need to. He had asked the same question in front of that sand table. The mayor’s answer was: move the government over there, and the people will follow.

But those several thousand people the government would move had already been living in town. When they moved from town to the North City, town would have several thousand flats emptied out. The total didn’t change. There weren’t more people, they were just shifted from here to there.

A closed tank: scoop the water from the left side to the right, and there’s no more water than before.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Gu Xuerong had said nothing the whole time.

She sat beside Ye Zhixing, still holding her controller. Her character was still standing in that rain-soaked corridor, not moving, the rain on the screen falling and falling.

Ye Zhixing turned his head and looked at her.

She looked back at him, so long he almost wanted to look away, before she spoke.

“Are you going to be toast? Right there?”

Ye Zhixing froze.

Su Tang and Chen Xi froze too, both turning their heads to look at her.

Gu Xuerong’s face was as flat as ever, as if she were asking for the answer to a problem. She looked at Ye Zhixing, her eyes very dark, very still, not blinking once.

“Those buildings,” she said. “Half built, and then they can’t go on. The pits they dug underneath.” She paused. “Will you be in there?”

The room was very quiet.

Ye Zhixing looked at her, his mouth opened, and nothing came out.

He found he had no answer.

He wanted to say no, he had his own company, his money wasn’t in there, he wouldn’t be buried. But he thought of what his father had said in the car, “It’s an admission ticket.” Thought of that nod his father had given him at the dinner. Thought of the director saying, “Your family’s building the new high school too, you’ll be studying in a school your own family built.”

He thought of three years ago.

Back then, he had also thought he was standing outside it.

Only later did he learn that the person standing at the very front is the one furthest inside.

“…I don’t know,” he said.

Gu Xuerong looked at him for a while.

Then she turned back and took a proper grip on her controller again.

“Then just run,” she said.

Her character moved on the screen, took one step forward, stopped, and looked back at his character, as if waiting for him.

## 6. The Mini-Program

That night, he woke in the middle of the night again.

Two-forty.

He didn’t go and sit in front of the aquarium. He turned on his computer.

The screen lit up, its bluish-white light on his face. He logged in to a back end.

The home page of the back end was a chart, one line, climbing from the bottom left to the top right, not climbing fast, but climbing the whole way. Under the chart were a few numbers: active users yesterday, total registered users, new posts yesterday, this month’s revenue from pinned posts and ads.

That was his mini-program.

It was called “Town Matters”. He had picked the name offhand in his last year of middle school, a very plain, folksy name, and later couldn’t be bothered to change it. At first it was just a local noticeboard: whose dog was lost, who wanted to rent out a flat, who wanted to sell a second-hand e-bike, post it up and everyone could see. Later he slowly divided it into sections: jobs, second-hand, homes to rent and buy, shops for transfer, carpools, lost and found, tutoring, public notices.

He didn’t do anything else with it. No food delivery, no errand running, never touching money passing from one person’s hands to another’s. It was just a board, a board a bit bigger and a bit cleaner than the telegraph poles and the noticeboards.

Now, almost everyone in the county town who used a smartphone had this mini-program on their phone. Labour contractors looking for workers for building sites posted jobs on it, restaurant owners looking for dishwashers posted jobs on it, university graduates just back in the county town looking for work scrolled through it post by post. When someone was moving away, they put their fridge and washing machine up, and within half a day someone came to haul them off; when someone’s child had outgrown a little bicycle, they put it up for twenty yuan, and underneath came a row of comments asking if it was still available. The woman who ran the copy shop had once put up the shopfront for transfer, left it up for a week and then took it down again, saying that when she thought about it, she couldn’t bear to let it go. Sister Mei had found a tutor for her child on it. Old Zhou had tried to hire a kitchen hand on it, didn’t find one, and said young people these days don’t like going into kitchens.

The thing made money.

The money came from three places. One was pinning: a post you put up would get pushed down by every new post after it, and if you wanted it to stay at the top, you paid, by the day, a few yuan a day. Two was ads: on the home page and in the middle of every section there were a few business ads slotted in, renovation companies, driving schools, cram schools, wedding photography, and each one had a small grey box in the top right corner, and in the box, one word: “Ad”, very small, but always there. Three was that some posts themselves cost money: the sections for jobs, shop transfers and home sales charged a tiny bit per post, while ordinary people selling an old fridge or looking for a lost dog paid nothing.

Ads had to be labelled: that was the very first rule he had set, earlier even than the line written on the wall when he opened the shop. Once a company selling health supplements came to him, offering five times what anyone else paid, on condition that it not be labelled “Ad” and made to look like an ordinary post. He turned it down.

It wasn’t much, but it kept earning. Bit by bit, added up, it was a very thin stream of water that had never once run dry.

Beyond Town Matters, the company also took on custom work: ordering systems for restaurants in the county and the city, membership points for supermarkets, booking systems for driving schools and gyms. That side brought in more money than Town Matters, each job a real sum, but every one had to be negotiated business by business.

This was his.

Not his father’s, not the Ye family’s, not a script someone had handed him. It was written by him line by line of code, negotiated by him business by business, fixed by him bug by bug.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

He stared at that number until the screen was about to lock itself.

Then he opened another file.

It was a spreadsheet. It listed the Ye family’s businesses: the building-materials company, the logistics fleet, the two developments, the plot in the west, and the North City. After each row were some marks he had made.

He was looking.

Looking for the places that could be plugged in.

The two developments in the east and south still had several hundred flats unsold, and every month they ran ads in the papers, on the TV station, on the sides of buses— those ads could go on “Town Matters”, on the home page, long term, labelled “Ad”. The Ye family’s building-materials company had hundreds of renovation crews and small contractors downstream, hiring all year round— those job posts could all go through “Town Matters”, charged per post. The developments’ property-management notices, water and power cuts, the flats owners wanted to sublet or resell, could also be gathered in the “homes to rent and buy” section. And if that new district in the North City really did get built, and several thousand households moved in, the ones looking for work, selling old furniture, looking for tutors, would all be on this board.

All of it was legal. All of it was normal business cooperation. The Ye family’s companies would pay to buy ad space and posting services from his company, the services were real, the prices were fair, the ads were all labelled “Ad”, the accounts were clean.

He scrolled the spreadsheet down to the very bottom, to the empty row, the cursor blinking in it.

He thought of what Chen Xi had said: “I’m leaving, as far as I can get.”

He couldn’t leave.

He skipped class and nobody did anything; he didn’t wear the uniform and nobody stopped him; he ran a cat café, wrote programs, did whatever he wanted. But his name was written on the same sheet of paper as those two developments, as the land in the North City, as the building with the red flag on the sand table.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

Outside the window, it was still dark.

The blue night light in the corner of the aquarium was on. The fish in the tank were asleep, hanging in the gaps between the plants, the blue lines along their sides flickering.

He closed the spreadsheet, opened a new page in the back end and began writing a partnership proposal. The title was “Annual Advertising and Job-Posting Partnership Proposal for Ye’s Building Materials and the East and South Developments”.

He wrote very fast, line after line, like doing a problem whose answer he had known all along.

Halfway through, his phone buzzed.

It was Gu Xuerong.

> still up  

It wasn’t a question.

He looked at the message for a while, and replied with one word:

> mm  

After a while, from the other end:

> me too  

> what are you doing  

> writing something  

> im mining  

After it came a screenshot. Stardew Valley, the mines, level seventy-three. Her character stood among a patch of rocks glowing purple, her backpack stuffed full, her health bar down to a sliver.

> stop mining youre about to die  

> mm  

> go back to bed  

> you too  

He looked at those few words.

He put the phone down, looked at the half-written proposal on the screen, looked out of the window, looked at the aquarium.

He saved the proposal, left the computer on, and the screen dimmed by itself.

He went back to bed and lay down. After a while he sat up again, opened “Town Matters” on his phone, and, with no particular purpose, just scrolled down. Jobs, second-hand, rentals, a few pinned posts hanging at the top, on a yellow background, a renovation company’s ad tucked in the middle, the small grey box in its top right corner saying “Ad”.

When he scrolled to the “tutoring” section, he stopped.

A post put up at eight-forty that evening, not pinned, already pushed down to fifth place by the posts after it:

> Girl in first year of high school, can tutor primary school Chinese and maths, good with kids, patient. Free weekend daytimes. 15 yuan an hour, negotiable. Contact: Su (student).  

Views: 3.

The phone number left at the bottom, he recognized. It was Su Tang’s.

He looked at that post. His finger rested on the screen, and right beside it was a “Pin” button; he was the admin of the back end, one tap and it wouldn’t cost a thing.

He didn’t tap it.

He put the phone back on the bedside table, screen down.

Outside the window, it had begun to snow.

# Chapter Twelve　Home Cooking

## 1. The Box

That Saturday afternoon, Ye Zhixing came up the stairs carrying a polystyrene box.

The box was big, the kind seafood comes in, white, a few chunks knocked off its four corners, wrapped round several times with wide tape. He carried it very carefully, both hands under the bottom, taking the stairs one at a time, much more slowly than usual. Something in the box was moving: click, click, like someone tapping on the polystyrene with a fingernail.

The copy-shop owner poked her head out of the glass door. “Young Ye, what have you got this time?”

“A crab.”

“A crab? In the middle of winter, where’d you get a crab?”

“Kept it at home.”

She craned her neck to try and see into the box, but the lid was on and she couldn’t see a thing, only hear click, click inside. She drew her head back in, muttered “rich people’s kids, always up to something,” and went back to her copying.

::: {.break custom-style="Scene Break"}
·  ·  ·
:::

There weren’t many people at the shop that day. It was snowing, the roads were slippery, and only two groups came: one ate and left, and the other was three middle-school girls lying on the open floor by the window, playing with Calico.

Su Tang was in the back room blow-drying the Devon. Gu Xuerong sat on the grey sofa doing the accounts, the ledger open on her knees, her pen twirling between two fingers. Chen Xi was there too, just come from the lab, still in his down jacket, squatting under the cat tree, locked in a contest of wills with Rice Cake over a feather wand. Rice Cake sat on the second level of the cat tree, eyes narrowed, watching the feather swing back and forth without moving at all, as if watching a not especially bright human put on a show.

Ye Zhixing set the polystyrene box on the floor by the counter and lifted the lid.

A cold breath rose out of it, briny, with a hint of seawater.

Chen Xi was the first one over. Gu Xuerong looked up and closed the ledger. In the back room the hairdryer stopped, and Su Tang came out holding the Devon wrapped in a towel, leaning over to look into the box.

The box was lined with a layer of soaking-wet sponge, and on the sponge sat a crab.

A very big one.
